#5667. How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Every September, Climate Week and Global Citizen Week in New York bring together policymakers, investors and innovators focused on the world’s most pressing problems.

It’s also when Cisco Systems Inc. and Global Citizen recognize the winner of the Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award. Cisco and Global Citizen created the award in 2018 to honor a young leader who uses technology to help end extreme poverty, and this year’s recipient may have the most compelling story yet.

Diana Virgovicova (pictured) is the founder and CEO of Xatoms (pronounced “X-Atoms”), a Toronto-based company that uses artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to design sunlight-activated materials that break down pollutants in water. The award comes with a $250,000 grant, and Xatoms was chosen from more than 2,000 applications.

Most of the AI conversation at Climate Week focused on what AI takes from the planet: power, land and, increasingly, water. Xatoms offers a positive counterpoint, a case study in AI giving back.

Most founders find a market. Virgovicova found a problem the hard way. She grew up in a village of about 800 people in Slovakia, surrounded by farms that used heavy amounts of pesticides. “I got sick when I was 14 years old,” she told me. “I was diagnosed with ovarian cancer because of the water I drank.”

After her diagnosis, she persuaded her mother to go backpacking across Asia. On trains in India, she heard from women facing the same thing. “I learned that there is a girl in Slovakia who got sick. There is a girl in India who’s getting infections. There is a girl in Africa who has to spend long hours every single day searching for clean water,” she said. “So, we need to find a solution, and it is affecting mainly women across the globe.”

Globally, women and girls spend 250 million hours a day collecting water, more than three times the time men and boys spend. “While boys go to school, the girls are responsible for bringing a bucket of water home, and they start missing school very early on,” Virgovicova explained. “It’s an educational, economic and health problem.”

And it’s growing. “We have 2 billion people that don’t have access to clean drinking water, and this number is actually growing because of flooding, climate change,” she said.

One of the more interesting aspects of Xatoms is where it chose to play. Many water treatment efforts target bacteria such as E. coli because the effects are immediate. Xatoms goes after the harder problem: complex industrial pollutants such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, forever chemicals and heavy metals.

“I think we are forgetting about these complex contaminants because they don’t make us sick tomorrow. They make us sick in 10 years,” she said. “They give us chronic diseases. They cause infertility.” She made a point I hadn’t considered: Scientific progress is making it worse.

“We are able to create better antibiotics, but these better antibiotics are more complex, thus more difficult to destroy in water,” she said. That’s a second-order problem traditional treatment wasn’t built for, and exactly where advanced computational design has an edge.

At 17, while working with a university professor in Slovakia, Virgovicova used quantum chemistry software to design a new molecule that harnesses sunlight to break down water pollutants. That work earned her a Diploma of Excellence from the Swedish Royal Family and a full scholarship to the University of Toronto.

“What is so exciting about this science is that we can use computers to design new materials, and we don’t have to create them in the lab,” she said. “We can see these materials, how they react, and what their properties are before we even synthesize them.”

Quantum chemistry gets far fewer headlines than quantum computing, so I asked her to explain it. “Quantum helps us understand these molecules at a fundamental level, including how the atoms within the molecule interact,” she said. “When we know these fundamental properties, we can understand what makes each molecule good at something, and that helps us design an even better molecule, a better material.”

The output is a photocatalyst powder. “Initially, it was a molecule in a computer, but we were able to synthesize it in a lab,” Virgovicova said. “We put this photocatalytic powder into water. It splits water into OH radicals, and the OH radicals then destroy contaminants.”

Because it’s a catalyst, it isn’t consumed, so a small amount can treat “hundreds of gallons,” she said. Earlier photocatalysts required ultraviolet light; her design works with visible light, such as sunlight or LEDs, eliminating the need for expensive UV reactors.

AI is the accelerant. “It would take a decade if we did it without AI,” she said. “We can do it in 30 days.” That’s the real story for business leaders. Materials discovery has historically been slow, expensive and lab-bound, and Xatoms has transformed it into a computational pipeline.

Here’s where it matters for technology buyers. Data centers consume enormous volumes of water for cooling, and the AI buildout is making that worse. I asked Virgovicova whether Xatoms can flip the script. “There are a lot of problems with contaminants within the data center,” she said. “The data center water needs to be completely clean for cooling,” she said. “We are able to use this catalyst to help reuse the water in data centers.”

This is an underappreciated opportunity. Hyperscalers and neoclouds face mounting pressure over water use, and the industry’s response has largely focused on cooling design. Reuse through improved treatment is a different and more planet-friendly solution.

Xatoms works with Indigenous communities in Canada under longstanding boil-water advisories, as well as in Kenya and South Africa. Virgovicova told me the footprint now includes Japan and Azerbaijan. Every engagement is customized.

“We collect a water sample. Recently, we shipped the sample from Azerbaijan all the way to Canada,” she said. “We identify the contaminant and then determine which of these 88 options would be the best.”

Customers define the outcome. “Some of them want to take yellow water and decolorize it. Some of them have a specific contaminant in mind that they want to remove or reduce,” she said.

Next up are Turkey, where co-founder Kerem Topal Ismail Oglou grew up, and the broader Middle East, driven by textile manufacturing and oil and gas. She also met South Africa’s water minister during Climate Week ahead of a trip to Cape Town.

Being named a global winner of the World Economic Forum’s Water Resilience Challenge opened doors with large enterprises. “We had the chance to interact with some of the biggest Fortune 500 companies, which helped us create pilots and partnerships,” she said.

The Cisco grant is moving directly into execution. “We have more than six major projects coming up, so we need help with lab work,” she said. “We need to figure out the best way to manufacture more materials.” The goal is to “commercialize this technology as fast as we can.”

When I joked that billionaires are hunting for water on Mars while we haven’t solved it here, she pointed out a funding gap. “About 3% of climate VC funding goes to water only,” she said. Water underpins industry, agriculture and now AI infrastructure, yet it remains capital-starved.

Virgovicova mentors young founders, especially women in science and climate, and her advice is very direct. “There’s always going to be skepticism in every single room you go into at first,” she said. “It’s very important that you know how to present yourself and that you’re confident. You can really prove everyone wrong as long as you know your stuff.” With women still scarce among Fortune 500 CEOs, she added, “If I can do it, you can do it as well.”

Her favorite piece of advice: “If you focus on watering your grass, you don’t care about someone’s grass being greener.” And the AI myth she wants gone? “That it’s going to destroy the world. I think it’s a tool for improving the world.”

Cisco uses this award to make a point it rarely gets credit for: technology’s value is measured by what it does for people. Xatoms applies two of the decade’s most hyped technologies, AI and quantum, to a tangible, urgent problem.

For technology leaders, there are three key takeaways. First, AI’s biggest payoff may come from scientific discovery, where compressing a decade of work into 30 days can reshape an entire industry’s economics. Second, AI’s water problem has solutions beyond cooling design, and data center builders should be evaluating treatment and reuse partners now. Third, water deserves far more capital than it receives.

In 10 years, Virgovicova wants Xatoms to be “a global leader in discovery of these materials,” with solutions for many toxic contaminants worldwide. Given how far she has come from a village of 800 people, I wouldn’t bet against her.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5666. Immigration Slowdown To Sharply Reduce Renter Household Growth, Study Says

The clampdown on immigration has slowed the nation's population growth. Now, Harvard estimates it is also slowing the formation of new households in the United States.

Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies estimates that immigration policy means 500,000 fewer households formed in the country each year from 2024 to 2027. Those 2 million households are mainly renters, but over time become homebuyers, Harvard said.

President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown has broad implications for the national housing market. People coming into the country on work and student visas are a major contributor to rental demand. Homebuilders rely on a significant immigrant workforce, and crackdowns have contributed to worsening builder sentiment.

Harvard researcher Daniel McCue said this marks a sharp turn from the 571,000 net new-renter households formed by immigrants who entered the country from 2022 to 2024 under President Joe Biden. At least one Fed study indicated illegal immigration may have driven up housing costs during the Biden administration.

Instead, McCue projected immigrants would account for just 132,000 new household formations by 2027.

This is based on the U.S. Census Bureau's most recent housing vacancy survey, which showed a marked increase in rental vacancy and a slowdown in new household formation overall. The national rental vacancy rate bumped from 7.1% in the third quarter of 2025 to 7.6% in the same time this year.

"This may be a sign that the sharp curtailment of immigration has begun to lower demand for rental units in a significant way," McCue said.

Jiayi Xu, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says such a slowdown could spell trouble for the housing market over the long term.

"A significant slowdown in immigration growth would cause household growth to slow over the next decade, dragging down economic growth in the long term," Xu says.

Eric Finnigan, vice president of demographics research for John Burns Research and Consulting, says the shifting immigration policies of Biden and Trump have led to disruptions in the housing market. Immigration has been a central pillar of the nation's population growth, and falling birthrates haven't kept up.

"We knew at the beginning of the decade, given our demographic trends, that immigration would be important to economic growth," Finnigan says. "That includes housing demand, labor supply, and homebuyers and renters. We didn't plan for this sharp surge in immigration nor a sharp decline."

In the past, immigrant populations have been an important contributor to the housing market. Students and workers on visas routinely generate demand for new rental properties. In time, some of those renters eventually become buyers. But, Finnigan says, the whiplash of the policies of recent years could chill demand at a time when the housing market is seeing fewer buyers.

"The rules about their own visa could change overnight without any warning," Finnigan adds. "The last thing they want to do is plunk down a down payment on a home or be on the hook for an asset they want to leave at some point. They don't want to be with an asset they might have to leave without warning."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5665. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

#5662. VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.

Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.

By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.

Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.

“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”

Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.

Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

#5661. Wall Street’s AI Sell-Off Exposes a Weak Spot in the Bank of Mom and Dad

As more adult children count on the Bank of Mom and Dad to help them buy homes, Mom and Dad, in turn, may be counting on Wall Street.

That arrangement looked a little less secure on Friday, when fears about the cost of the artificial intelligence boom sent stocks tumbling.

The Nasdaq lost 2.9% on Oct. 30, its worst day since June, as investors grew worried about the billions of dollars companies are spending on AI. Intel shares plunged 28.6%, while chipmakers AMD and Nvidia fell 10.9% and 4.2%, respectively, according to Reuters.

The consequences could reach well beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Baby boomers held approximately $35.2 trillion in stocks and mutual funds as of the second quarter of 2026, or roughly 55% of the household total, according to Federal Reserve data analyzed by Yardeni Research.

And some of that money is already making its way into their children's down payments. Half of parents who had helped or planned to help their children purchase a home reported drawing on investment accounts, according to an April survey by Veterans United Home Loans.

Of course, one bad day won't drain the Bank of Mom and Dad. But if the losses keep piling up, the damage could spill out of parents' portfolios. Research shows that after substantial financial setbacks, parents tend to scale back the money they give their adult children—or stop giving it altogether.

The AI boom has played an enormous role in the stock market's recent run. Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, AI-related stocks accounted for roughly 75% of S&P 500 returns, according to a JPMorgan analysis.

And that rally has helped swell the fortunes of a generation already poised to pass down an extraordinary amount of wealth.

Approximately $105 trillion will pass to heirs through 2048, according to estimates from the weath management firm Cerulli Associates—with baby boomers and older generations accounting for the vast majority of the projected transfer.

But some of that money is changing hands much sooner, as parents and grandparents help adult children overcome the financial barriers to homeownership.

Nearly one-quarter of parents surveyed by Veterans United expected to contribute between $50,000 and $99,999 toward their children's home purchases, while 12% anticipated providing between $100,000 and $199,999.

They're shocking sums, and years of rising stock prices may have made those commitments easier to make.

"When their stock portfolios go up, they feel more able to help with a down payment," says Michelle Riehn, a certified financial planner and founder of Money Momma. "People feel richer."

The trouble is that those feelings—and the financial resources behind them—can change when markets fall.

In a 2025 study published in The Review of Economics and Statistics, economists Jessamyn Schaller and Chase Eck examined how financial transfers between parents and adult children changed following setbacks such as wealth losses, job exits, and health problems.

They found that parents sharply reduced financial assistance following losses of wealth and earned income, particularly in households with fewer accumulated assets.

An earlier working-paper version estimated that among lower-wealth households, a major loss of net worth reduced the likelihood of parents making a financial transfer by 6.1 percentage points, or 18.7% relative to the group's baseline rate.

The research examined financial assistance broadly, not just down payments, and didn't isolate stock market losses. Still, the findings have important implications for housing, where financial help from parents can make the difference between buying a home and remaining a renter.

Already, parental transfers account for 13 percentage points, or 27%, of young households' homeownership, according to a 2025 Federal Reserve working paper.

Naturally, the next question for a generation waiting on those transfers is what happens if AI stocks continue to fall.

Friday's slide was far from the end of the AI boom. Despite losing more than $1 trillion in market value that day, technology stocks were still worth trillions, with Nvidia alone valued at roughly $4.9 trillion.

But researchers have examined what a much larger reversal could mean for U.S. households.

In September, Allianz Research modeled the consequences of disappointing AI investments triggering a broader market downturn.

Under its more severe scenario, a 25% decline in the S&P 500 would erase approximately $27 trillion in U.S. household wealth—nearly 14% of total household net worth—and help push the economy into recession.

That's a hypothetical scenario, not a forecast. And even losses of that magnitude wouldn't affect every family's ability to help their children equally.

Financial advisers say much depends on whether parents have already set aside the money they intend to give—or are counting on their investments to cover the gift when the time comes.

"There's a difference between help that was planned and requests that come unplanned," Riehn says.

Parents who have committed to helping their children buy homes often move that money into conservative investments well before the purchase, she explains. Doing so can shield a planned gift from a sudden drop in stock prices.

But when parents haven't prepared, a downturn can force tougher decisions.

"A lot of times they're selling stock to do it, and that's where it gets tricky in a downturn," says Greg Black, a certified financial planner and president of Tencap Wealth Coaching in Utah.

A parent who expected to sell appreciated investments to cover a $100,000 down payment might have to liquidate more shares after a substantial market decline. Rather than lock in those losses, the parent could decide to reduce the gift or postpone it.

"So if the down payment money is sitting in AI stocks and they drop, that gift might have to wait," Black says.

Even parents who could still afford to help may think twice. Riehn says watching a portfolio lose value can make affluent households more reluctant to part with money, particularly when their children make unexpected requests.

David Talley, a certified financial planner with Talley Wealth in Johnson City, TN, offers a counterpoint: Families with sufficient cash reserves and diversified investments should generally be able to maintain gifts that fit within their long-term financial plans.

"With the cash layer in place, the gift doesn't have to wait for a recovery," he says.

But younger homebuyers might not have that flexibility.

Allianz estimated that a 15% market correction could take six to nine months to reverse under one scenario. In its more severe scenario, recovering from a 25% decline could take as long as two years.

That extended timeline points to another potential consequence of an AI bust: Any prolonged downturn could also change what parents expect to leave their children.

In an earlier working-paper version of their research, Schaller and Eck found that a major household wealth loss was associated with roughly a 5-percentage-point decline in parents' reported probability of leaving an inheritance worth at least $100,000.

That finding measures parents' expectations, not the inheritances their children ultimately received. And the consequences of a market correction would depend partly on how much of a family's wealth is tied to the stocks losing value.

"The real exception is a family with a concentrated position in one company whose net worth has doubled in a few years," Talley says. "That genuinely changes what they can give."

And if those gains reverse, so can the amount available to pass down.

Still, Riehn cautions that inheritances operate on a different timeline from down payment gifts. Children expecting to inherit investments decades from now may have time to ride out a market downturn. Those counting on that wealth for a home purchase in the nearer future may not.

The recent AI sell-off is far from a market crash, and there's no evidence it has already disrupted parental gifts or inheritances. Instead, it highlights an uncertainty at the heart of the Great Wealth Transfer: The fortunes younger Americans expect to receive aren't necessarily the fortunes their parents will ultimately leave behind.

And until that money changes hands, the next generation has little control over how much will be there—or when it will arrive.

#5660. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5659. Confused by Home Price Headlines? Here’s Why.

Whether you own a house already or you’re looking to buy one, you probably care about home prices. But it’s not always easy to figure out what’s really happening right now, especially if you look at the headlines.

One says home prices are falling. The next says they’re still climbing.

So, which one’s right? It comes down to where you live.

Part of the confusion out there may be based on what’s happening to asking prices and how the media is talking about it. They’re calling attention to how asking prices are falling, but don’t give the full context or say that seasonality is at play. So here it is.

Right now, there are more homes on the market than at any other time since November 2019. And with mortgage rates rising since the spring, those homes are taking a little longer to sell. One way to help a home sell quickly in that environment is to have a lower asking price.

According to HousingWire Data, the median asking price is down from $449k in early August to $435k just 2 months later (see graph below):

That’s a dip of about 3%, and a lot of it is normal for this time of year.

Asking prices cool off every fall once the busy summer season wraps up. With fewer buyers this time of year, sellers price a bit more competitively. Today’s rates play a role too, since sellers are pricing to match what buyers can afford right now. And that’s a good thing. Smart pricing helps homes sell.

Just keep in mind, that’s a national list price. It doesn’t show what homes near you are actually selling for. So before you react to a headline, ask a local agent what’s really happening in your area.

“While national headlines might suggest a buyer’s market is taking hold, the reality on the ground depends heavily on where and what you’re trying to buy. Local trends can diverge sharply from national averages, especially when you factor in price range, property type, and post-pandemic market dynamics.”

The latest numbers from S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index show how true that is. Over the past year, sales prices in Chicago rose almost 7%. In Seattle, they dipped about 1.6%. That’s a gap of nearly 9 percentage points between two major cities (see graph below):

That gap changes your game plan. Selling in New York, where prices are up almost 6%? You may not need to cut your price. Buying in Denver or Las Vegas? You may have more room to negotiate.

Just in case you’re seeing those slight declines in some markets and worried it means a bigger crash is coming, here’s what you need to remember. Even in the major metros where prices are down, the declines are 2% or less. That’s a long way from a crash like 2008. And if you look back at the graph above, there are more cities in the green than in the red.

And over time, home values have a strong track record. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) says national prices have grown year-over-year every quarter since 2012. Go back further, and a $100k home bought in 1991 would be worth about $436k today, even with the 2008 crash factored in (see graph below):

So, this short-term dip probably won’t stick around. The small declines we’re seeing now are in markets that overheated during the pandemic. As a whole, the market is headed back to normal – and normal means prices should rise over time.

National headlines can’t tell you what your home is worth or how much room you have to negotiate. Local data can. If you’re thinking about buying or selling, connect with a local real estate agent to look at how prices are moving in your area, so you can set your price or make your offer with confidence.

#5658. Why a Long Island Town’s Crackdown on Vacation Rentals May Not Fix Its Housing Crisis

The four-bedroom waterfront home on Long Island's North Fork hadn't even hit the market when Diane Mollica's colleagues began imagining another use for it.

"Several of them commented that it would be a fabulous rental property because it has all of the perks that you want on vacation," Mollica, a real estate agent with the Gambino Group at Compass, tells Realtor.com®.

It was easy enough to see their point: Beyond walls of glass stood a swimming pool, a sandy beach, and the sparkling blue waters of the Long Island Sound. Upstairs, a rooftop deck offered yet another picturesque view.

But Southold, the town encompassing much of the North Fork, wants fewer homes operating as short-term rentals.

A newly proposed permit lottery would allow just 119 properties across the town's North Fork hamlets to offer stays shorter than 30 days—that's less than one-fifth of the 640 active vacation-rental listings in October.

Officials hope the regulation would help protect residential neighborhoods from revolving vacation guests and preserve housing for people who live and work there year-round. But research from cities that have tried similar restrictions shows mixed results.

Mollica knows what draws people to the North Fork. Roughly 25 years ago, she came from Brooklyn for a weekend and ended up buying a house herself.

"What I love about the North Fork is the people are very embracing. They're very community-minded," she says.

The area has long attracted weekenders and summer vacationers, but the COVID-19 pandemic brought a wave of newcomers who began putting down more permanent roots.

"People made a mad rush to the North Fork because they saw the opportunity really to live and not to shelter in place," Mollica recalls. "They enrolled their children in school. They got to know their friends and neighbors. ... So a lot of those people stayed."

Others eventually returned to the city while keeping their North Fork properties as second homes, leaving year-round residents, seasonal homeowners, and vacationers with competing visions for the community.

At an October civic forum, residents complained about pool parties, weddings, traffic, and unfamiliar guests coming and going.

"I'm in a residential community; this is where I want to live," one resident told officials. "I don't want to live in a business district."

Then there's the growing difficulty of affording a home at all.

By the end of 2025, the median price of a single-family home on the North Fork had reached a record $999,000—more than eight times Southold Town's median household income of $116,667. Meanwhile, an estimated 54% of town renters spent at least 30% of their incomes on housing, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

Even Town Councilwoman Alexa Suess, a Greenport native who campaigned on affordability, recently said she would have to move after her landlord raised her rent above $4,000 a month.

"I don't know anybody my age who I went to school with that is still here," she told a September housing forum.

Naturally, that friction has put a renewed spotlight on the town's massive share of vacation properties: Nearly 37% of its housing stock consisted of seasonal residences in 2020, according to the town's 2023 Community Housing Plan.

At first glance, those seasonal homes might seem like a natural solution for Southold's problems: a reservoir of untapped housing just waiting to be unleashed. But the town's own experience regulating vacation rentals reveals just how difficult it can be to turn those properties into year-round housing.

The town banned stays shorter than 14 nights in 2015, but officials have struggled to enforce the rule. Its housing plan subsequently identified vacation rentals as one possible contributor to the shortage.

Now, officials want to go further, requiring permits for stays shorter than 30 days, limiting them to 1% of single-family homes in each hamlet, and strengthening enforcement. The proposed system could begin in January 2028, although lawmakers have yet to formally adopt it.

The question is what happens to those homes once renting them out becomes more difficult.

Asked whether the cap could flood Southold's for-sale market, Mollica replies: "I'm going to say no."

Many of her clients already prefer monthlong or summer rentals, and she cautions that she works with few buyers seeking properties solely for rental income.

"Our clientele really come out to enjoy their home," she says. "They spend their summers here. They're looking forward to Thanksgiving and other holiday vacations here."

She recalls one family that moved back to New York City for personal reasons but kept their North Fork house as a second home. While they initially sought longer seasonal renters, they turned to Airbnb when finding tenants proved difficult.

"They wanted to rent it [out] ... to supplement their income in order to carry the mortgage," she explains.

And that supplemental income can be substantial.

Average summer nightly rates in Southold's vacation-rental market climbed from $463 in 2019 to $764 in 2026, a 65% increase, according to an analysis of AirDNA data provided to Realtor.com. Yet the median summer reservation lasted just three nights. The figures cover ZIP-code-based North Fork markets, including separately regulated Greenport Village.

"A 30-night minimum removes the weekend and short-stay premium, and a whole-season lease must cover all of an owner's income in a single booking," says Bram Gallagher, AirDNA's director of economics and forecasting.

It's true that owners may decide that renting out their homes is no longer worth the trouble. But that doesn't mean they'll sell or make those properties available to year-round tenants.

Alexander Marsella, an economist at Berry College, says the outcome depends on an owner's next best use of the property.

If that alternative is "a second home for the family," he says, "then restricting short-term rentals isn't going to do much to improve housing affordability."

Research from cities that have already restricted vacation rentals suggests he's right. A 2024 study of Berlin found that the crackdown targeting only commercial operators—not occasional hosts—significantly increased long-term rental supply.

New York City saw a similar disconnect. Short-term listings on Airbnb fell 87% after its 2023 crackdown, but rents barely budged and conventional rental inventory showed no unusual increase, according to Marsella's August 2026 working paper, which has not yet undergone peer review.

And Marsella suspects the effect on year-round housing could be even smaller in a seasonal market.

"If I don't see it happening in New York City so much, I feel like I would be less likely to see it happen in a seasonal market," he says.

Town officials have already acknowledged that restricting vacation rentals won't necessarily determine what happens to the properties themselves.

"Owners are going to have to make a decision about what to do with the houses," Planning Director Heather Lanza said in 2024. "They can go to summer rentals or year-round."

At Mollica's waterfront listing, that decision will soon belong to someone new.

The four-bedroom home is preparing to hit the market, and prospective buyers may already waiting.

"I have several people that are waiting for the right property," Mollica says.

Its swimming pool, private beach access, and sweeping views of Long Island Sound make it an enticing vacation retreat. But those same qualities could appeal to someone looking to put down permanent roots.

Mollica herself came to the North Fork for a weekend nearly 25 years ago and ended up staying.

The next buyer might do the same—or simply return for summer vacations. Southold's proposed rules could influence how the property is used, but whether it becomes a year-round home will ultimately be the buyer's decision.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5657. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. A smart sales strategy can help your house stand out to buyers from day one.So, if you’re on the fence, a local real estate agent can help you compare what selling and renting would each look like for you.

#5656. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5655. Pregnant Savannah Chrisley Announces She’s Expecting a Baby Boy With Husband Jason Galanis: ‘Our Sweet Miracle’

TV personality Savannah Chrisley has revealed she and her husband, Jason Galanis, are expecting a baby boy.

Chrisley, 29, took to Instagram to share the joyous news of their baby's gender, just days after announcing that she and Galanis, 56, had said "I do" in a secret wedding.

“It's a boy! My sweet miracle boy, you are everything we prayed for and more. The most beautiful reminder that God’s plans are always greater than our own,” she captioned the Instagram post.

In the video, the couple could be seen laying on a blanket and embracing each other.

It then cut to them cutting a white cake that read "baby" to reveal the blue icing inside.

They then posed with Chrisley's mom, Julie Chrisley, and her dad, Todd Chrisley, who was previously imprisoned with Galanis.

"The past few days have reminded me just how cruel this world can be. But no amount of hate could ever overshadow the joy of loving you. You are a MIRACLE. My precious baby boy, your daddy and I will spend the rest of our lives protecting you, praying over you, and loving you beyond measure. We may not be able to shield you from every bit of darkness in this world, but we promise to raise you to be a LIGHT in it.You are already our greatest blessing, our answered prayer, and the sweetest chapter of our lives," the mom to be penned in the caption.

She ended the post with the words, "God knew what He was doing when He gave us YOU. We get to be your mommy and daddy."

The 29-year-old real estate agent, who shot to fame alongside her parents on their reality TV show, "Chrisley Knows Best," announced on Oct. 27 that she was both pregnant and engaged to Galanis, who is 27 years her senior and served time behind bars alongside her father.

Days later, it was revealed that they are actually married, with People reporting that they said "I do" on July 14—just one year after beginning their romance.

During an appearance on "The Golden Ticket," Chrisley admitted that the couple avoided filing their marriage paperwork in the U.S. so that they could keep the news to themselves.

“I’m not public about anything. We ended up getting married in the Cayman Islands in July. So we did everything there, but we haven’t filed [in the U.S.] because then it will be public record, right?" she said.

Despite having already tied the knot, she revealed that they plan to have another celebration in May.

“The wedding is in May. The wedding was supposed to be in January, [but] I have a real-life wedding crasher,” she said as she motioned toward her baby bump.

It was previously revealed that the couple began putting roots down for their family home months before she announced her pregnancy, with the soon-to-be parents picking up a $2.2 million pad in February, as first reported by TMZ.

The 5,207-square-foot property was built in 2023 and comes with five bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. It includes two fireplaces, chic wood and marble flooring, walk-in closets, and a chef's kitchen with state-of-the-art appliances.

It also features a patio, balcony, and two-car garage.

The home was listed for $2.9 million in June 2025, meaning the expectant mother got over a half-million dollars off.

After her husband's identity was revealed, Chrisley opened up about their romance on her podcast, "Unlocked," telling her fans that she doesn't pay any mind to their large age gap.

"Yes, there is a huge age gap there, OK? And that’s probably part of the reason why I kept a lot of it quiet, because I know how brutal the public can be. But I genuinely do not care," she insisted.

"I have always said, ‘I would rather [have] 20 phenomenal, unbelievable years with someone than 50 ‘meh’ years.' Like, the amount of love and respect that we have, we have so many dreams, and we dream together, we work together ... we want to have life experiences with each other. And I think that’s when you know you have the right person, when you don’t feel like you have to escape them at times. We do everything together. ... And it’s just such an amazing, fulfilling feeling to finally find your person. And I’m there. So, yes, the age difference. So what?"

Chrisley also shed some light on his proposal, which came a mere five months into their relationship.

"When he gave me the ring, he was like, ‘Before I open this, I just want you to know that this is just an expression of love to you. This can be whatever you want it to be. This can be an engagement ring, a promise ring, a cocktail ring for all I care. I just want you to know how much I love you,'" she said. "And there was no pressure ever put on me to, like, ‘You have to accept this as this.'"

Although she acknowledged that the engagement took place fairly early in their relationship, she added, "timing means nothing."

Chrisley announced the news of her pregnancy on Oct. 27 via an adorable Instagram post.

“I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine. And just when I thought my heart couldn’t hold any ›more love, God gave us our sweetest blessing yet ... we’re having a BABY!," Chrisley said in the social media post announcing the news, which saw her cradling her baby bump while sitting on her kitchen island and kissing Galanis.

“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever ... if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again. And then God sent me J," she added.

“My protector. My fiercest fighter. My most loyal person. My lover. My safe place. A man with the patience of Job (and Lord knows he needs it). The one who makes me laugh even on my hardest days. For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you," Chrisley said.

The TV personality then took a moment to praise her partner for how caring he has been during her pregnancy: “J, watching the way you already love and protect our baby before he/she has even entered this world has made me fall in love with you in an entirely new way. Not a single doctor’s appointment missed. Constantly caring for me, talking about our baby, and reminding me how beautiful my growing bump is. I thank God every day that this baby gets to call you Daddy."

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words. From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him. Only God could have written this story. Here’s to forever, J ... and the sweetest little blessing we can’t wait to meet," she added.

Chrisley had kept the identity of her partner under wraps until now, having previously revealed on her podcast, "Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley,"  that she wouldn't share his name "until after I'm married."

In the latest episode of her podcast, she revealed she and Jason began their romance last July, branding it a "dream relationship."

She revealed that Galanis proposed five months into their relationship when they were in the Cayman Islands. "The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted."

She then revealed that the couple connected after Jason reached out to her to praise her for her efforts to get her parents out of prison.

Todd and Julie Chrisley were found guilty in 2022 of conspiring to defraud Georgia banks out of more than $36 million in personal loans and tax evasion, before being pardoned by President Donald Trump in May 2025.

Savannah Chrisley has frequently spoken out about the toll of her parents' incarceration.

Todd, 57, was sentenced to 12 years (later reduced to 10 years) in the Federal Correctional Institution Pensacola in Florida. Julie, 53, was sentenced to seven years in the Federal Medical Center in Lexington, KY.

Following her parents' incarceration, Savannah took on the care of her brother, Grayson, 19, and her niece, Chloe, 13, while also assuming responsibility for the care and maintenance of her parents' opulent dwelling.

At the same time, the burgeoning real estate agent was tirelessly campaigning for Todd and Julie's release, issuing public pleas for government support, while alleging that her parents were being subjected to "beyond inhumane" conditions behind bars.

On May 27, her prayers were answered when Trump revealed to her in a personal phone call that he planned to pardon her parents. Just a few days later, they were released from prison.

At the time, Savannah revealed she was ready to return the hefty upkeep of their home to Todd and Julie.

#5654. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? Talk to a loan officer to find out.

#5653. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. #5652. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.
