#5628. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Find a New Home Base in the Cotswolds

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly moved into a new Cotswolds home on their friend's estate.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who moved to the U.K. in August with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, have been settling into their new lives across the pond.

After making the move, the couple was living "in the main house" of their pal's sprawling property.

However, now, their living situation has reportedly changed, with the Daily Mail reporting that they have moved onto another property "on the estate."

According to the outlet, the friend is a wealthy businessman who Harry, 42, befriended through their mutual support for various charities.

Harry and Markle were rumored to have been house hunting, with several reports noting that the former actress was even looking to replicate the luxury they had in their Montecito mansion.

The duchess reportedly wants the U.K. residence to boast nine bedrooms—the same number as their California estate—as well as plenty of luxurious amenities.

The news of their move came mere weeks after Harry opened up about their decision to leave California behind  and relocate their family to the U.K., revealing that their children's education and his desire to reconnect with his roots played a major role in the decision.

In an interview with GQ that was filmed in September but released only recently, Harry explained that the opportunity to enroll his children in British schools was particularly meaningful to him.

“Opportunities for the family, being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn’t know how important it was to me,” he said.

“I always thought it was going to be something that I would try to do or that we would try to do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it, and it’s just giving them a whole different experience.”

Harry emphasized that his decision was not a criticism of the U.S. education system, but rather an opportunity for Archie and Lilibet to experience life in two different countries.

“I’m not criticizing American schools, but I think for kids at 7 and 5 to be able to have that comparison and to have two completely different cultural experiences is so important today,” he explained.

Beyond their education, Harry said returning to Britain has allowed his children to spend more time with relatives and develop closer relationships with family friends.

Another motivation for the move, he explained, was to “be back closer to my family and to be back on U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there.

“It’s been nice to be close to friends, family, friends and friends and their children as well, to be able to have endless playdates to really, like, help our kids settle in," he said.

Despite the significance of the relocation, Harry admitted that he and Meghan, 45, had not necessarily mapped out the move years in advance.

“For us, when certain stars align, and it’s clear that this should or probably will end up being the case, then we lean into that,” he said.

After spending six years living in California, he said he increasingly wanted his children to become familiar with the country where he spent his own childhood.

“Having been here for six years now and only being able to go back to the U.K. for short periods of time, to actually have my whole family there with me, the place that I grew up, wanting to be able to show my kids where I grew up and have them have the experiences to some extent that I had—the good rather than necessarily the bad—provided real, proper, serious thinking as to, ‘This is an opportunity, let’s do it now,’” he said.

Harry also addressed his complicated history with the British press, expressing hope that his family's return could mark the beginning of a more positive chapter.

“Once you’ve been through it, once you’ve been able to talk about it and raise awareness to it, then people see it for what it is, which makes the environment slightly easier,” he said.

“And it’s not going to necessarily stop the behavior, but then that’s the second part, which is the behavior: My hope is that it will change.”

The duke acknowledged that tensions have persisted in the years since he and Meghan stepped back from their roles as senior working royals, but suggested he would welcome an opportunity to move forward.

“What happened back then was then, what’s happened over the last six years has been a continuation of that. There are some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that,” he said.

He added that he hopes both his family and the British media can put certain disputes behind them.

“I am optimistic. I’m hopeful,” Harry said. “I’m not naive. I have been naive in the past. But I think it’s important to remain optimistic.”

The interview surfaced just days after Harry and Meghan made their first official joint appearance in the U.K. since their relocation.

On Oct. 15, the couple traveled to Nottingham, England, where they greeted approximately 100 people during a public engagement.

The pair also spent time interacting with local schoolchildren, crouching down to speak with them. Meghan was presented with flowers and a balloon during the visit.

"It's great to be back," she told one person.

The warm welcome was filled with several special moments, including one that saw the crowd shouting, "I love you Duchess Meghan."

The appearance marked their return to a city that played an important role in their early relationship, having served as the location of their first official joint engagement following their November 2017 engagement announcement.

Their outing came days after it was reported that they were turning their attention to their professional and charitable commitments after spending their first several weeks in Britain adjusting to their new surroundings.

Their latest chapter comes more than six years after the couple stepped away from their roles as working members of the royal family and established a new life in North America.

The visit came as an insider close to the couple told People that Harry and Meghan are eager to devote more attention to their philanthropic endeavors, having initially concentrated on helping their children adapt to living in a new country.

Their transition has not been without complications.

According to the outlet, Archie and Lilibet were forced to change schools just two days into the academic year due to security and logistical concerns surrounding their commute.

However, the children have reportedly adapted to their new environment, allowing their parents to devote additional time to commitments outside the family home.

A source told People that Harry and Meghan have established a schedule centered around their children's school hours, while continuing to prioritize spending time together as a family.

#5627. Holiday Snow Forecast Reveals Which Lucky Homeowners Will Wake Up to a White Christmas This Year

November is in full swing, and if you’re starting to map out your holiday travel and winter maintenance game plan ahead of December, The Old Farmer’s Almanac has released its annual snowfall forecast for Christmas Day.

While it’s a long-held tradition to hold out hope for a “white” Christmas, this year might not see as many flurries as in years past.

It really depends on where you live—and if you do live somewhere with snow in the forecast, the time to secure your home from the elements is now.

The National Weather Service officially defines a white Christmas as having at least 1 inch of snow on the ground at 7:00 a.m. on Dec. 25.

With a super El Nino this year, conditions will look incredibly mixed come the holiday season.

For example, the publication predicts a white Christmas in the Northeast, for places like Vermont and upstate New York. But just below that in New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania, there isn’t even a chance of snowfall.

Other areas that can bank on snow this Christmas include the Intermountain region (like Colorado and Wyoming), and Alaska, while other regions, including the Pacific Northwest, High Plains, Lower Lakes, and the Ohio Valley, have a "chance of a white Christmas."

On the flip side, and perhaps not surprisingly, states in the Atlantic Corridor, the Southeast, Florida, the Deep South, the Upper Midwest, Heartland, Texas-Oklahoma, the Desert Southwest, and the Pacific Southwest are not expected to have a white Christmas

Regardless of whether you’re in for a white Christmas, if you live in an area that gets snow, you’ll likely see snow at some point this season.

The Farmers' Almanac is advising homeowners to prepare for a winter of “snow, sleet, and surprises” through March 2027.

Additionally, according to the NOAA, an El Niño system, like the one that’s been brewing since July, tends to be strongest during the winter months. But because of the strength of the system being tracked this year, there are plenty of variables at play.

“Every El Niño is not the same; each one is unique with its own imprint on our weather,” say Ken Graham, director, NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS). "Advanced monitoring and an improved understanding of El Niño patterns allow the NWS to better predict and better prepare the public and our core partners for what is to come.”

If a snowstorm is forecasted for your area in the coming months, as a homeowner, there are some important precautions you can take.

For starters, pipes leading to outdoor faucets and hoses are particularly vulnerable to damage when the temperature plummets, so it's crucial that you make turning them all off part of prepping for a snowstorm, even if you have little time to spare. So be sure to shut off the inside valves leading out to them, unhook hoses, and run your outdoor faucets to drain any water that might be hiding within.

You should also give some thought to your inside pipes to keep them from bursting as well. One smart way to prevent burst pipes indoors, keep cabinet doors under sinks open so warm air in your home can reach them more easily.

Also, before a storm settles in, make sure to clean your gutters. Debris in gutters can lead to ice dams, causing roof damage, which is the last thing you want when a storm hits.

Finally, a good rule of thumb is to seal any drafty windows. With utility prices as an all-time high, windows become a prime spot for energy loss.

“Seal out the cold using a shrink film window kit. This can block drafts and air leaks that lead to high heating costs,” says Randi Bujnovsky, weatherization product manager at Duck, a home weatherization brand in Cleveland.

Shrink film window kits are readily available online or at your local home improvement store. Just make sure you read the directions carefully before using one.

#5625. California Voters Could Approve ‘Secondary Mortgages.’ Can the Golden State Solve the Housing Crisis?

Lawmakers and advocates have made many attempts recently to address the affordability crisis that pervades the housing market—some more impactful than others. Legislative bodies have enacted laws addressing private listings, while President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order aimed at cutting costs for title and mortgage insurance and manufactured housing.

In tomorrow’s general election, California voters will vote on a meaningful and unique new measure that essentially allows first-time buyers to borrow the bulk of their down payment, theoretically removing a big barrier to homeownership (with several caveats).

California Proposition 37—or the Second Mortgage Homebuyer Program and Revenue Bond Initiative—would create an assistance program for first-time homebuyers, offering them loans that could cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, meaning a buyer only needs to put 3% down to reach the 20% threshold needed to avoid mortgage insurance.

One of the primary sponsors of the initiative, former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg spoke with RISMedia and desired for more California residents to achieve homeownership.

“We’re really underhoused in California, so much of the focus has been on subsidized tax supported rental housing. I don’t take that away for a second, but we haven’t done a really good job at making sure that middle-class folks—the missing middle—are able to buy a house,” he says.

The initiative would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to offer secondary mortgage loans for down payments, to eligible buyers.

To qualify for the program, applicants must have been residents of California for at least one year, agree to occupy the home as a primary residence within 60 days of closing, fall under the middle-income buyer threshold and provide a down payment of no less than 3% of the purchase price of the qualified homes.

The proposition is aimed at “middle-income buyers,” or buyers who have an income at or below 200% of the area median income.

A qualified home includes any “newly constructed homes, townhouses, row houses, condominiums, or manufactured homes, or a condominium or other residence in a nonresidential building repurposed for residential use, where the borrower is the first purchaser,” according to the proposition.

Within these limitations, the program theoretically allows buyers to put down much less while still getting the keys (the 3% down payment still comes out to around $17,000 for a median-priced new home in the state).

As for the $25 billion in bonds, Hertzberg emphasizes that funding does not rely on taxpayer wallets, but rather investors. What’s more, the bonds will be recycled continuously.

“The bottom line is, it’s evergreen. Evergreen means that it’s not over. When you pay off the loan, it’s evergreen and the money goes back out to somebody else,” Hertzberg notes. “Thirty years from now when all these initial loans are paid off, there’ll be brand new loans. We hired a professor from UCLA who analyzed it and said that it’ll raise $150 billion in new construction and 190,000 new homes.”

Michael Lane—state policy director at the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association (SPUR)—approves the initiative because it focuses on new homes.

“There are some programs the state has implemented which are just down payment assistance programs without creating new housing,” he asserts. “You’re actually just creating—with those programs—more demand for the existing housing stock, which means more competition which will also boost prices. We think it’s important for this to focus on new construction as well as the down payment assistance.”

Within the proposition, a “secondary mortgage” is a somewhat unique concept. In this case, a secondary mortgage refers to the loan offered to qualified homebuyers, of which goes toward a home’s down payment.

“This is different from a second mortgage,” David Garcia, deputy director of Policy at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation UC Berkeley, stated.

A website made by supporters of the proposition contains a tool that allows voters to view median home price by each county in California, and uses data provided by the California Association of Realtors®.

As with many coastal states, California has a divided housing market. According to the latest data, California metros were not immune to the effects of elevated mortgage rates, as pending home sales fell even in high activity cities such as San Francisco and San Jose.

Construction has fared no better, as the latest report from The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Census Bureau shows that housing starts in the West are down over 23% monthly, and down 25% from the previous year.

In that context, Proposition 37 is particularly relevant as the state seeks to sustainably increase housing that is affordable in a market that is both land constrained and highly regulated.

“We’re also focused on construction defect liability reform and liquidated damages for condominiums in California,” Lane notes. “We’re at a disadvantage compared to other states; it makes it more risky to build condominiums here. That’s why we don’t produce very many—about 3,000 developments of five units or more—compared to other states and nations which do 10 times that amount with lesser populations.”

Homebuilders cite global tensions and labor shortages for faltering construction rates. Although the conclusion of each year typically ushers in a slowdown in housing activity, the latest data for new-home sales showcases further deceleration, likely caused by high mortgage rates and economic unease.

The Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley does not take positions on bills or legislation. But Garcia does note that the initiative may encourage more than buyers.

“By limiting the use of funds to newly built housing, it also may act as an incentive for builders to build more homes that are for sale,” he says.

Although his focus is on housing in Sacramento, Lane points out that California’s homeownership rates leave much to be desired.

“We have one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation here in California because of our high housing costs and the median home price of over $800,000; it makes it very difficult for working families to scrape together the 20% down payment,” he notes.

Notably, California is one of only a few states where new homes are cheaper than existing homes, making Proposition 37 potentially more powerful at addressing affordability.

Lane also believes that more changes to California’s housing market will come, specifically by drawing investors and builders to the state.

“We’ve been working on this issue for decades and will continue to do so; there’s always more to do,” Lane says. “In California, the cost of construction and the rules for project approvals can make it very difficult and time-consuming. That’s why investors oftentimes look for other opportunities rather than investing in housing in California. We’ll continue to make it more business-friendly and friendly for housing construction.”

With five years’ worth of work nearing its climax, Hertzberg states that his goal with Prop 37 is to encourage the supply of affordable homes, in the hopes of addressing California’s low homeownership rates.

“It’s the simplest rule in economics, supply and demand,” he adds. “You get more supply, it works better. People can say all the arguments they want to make, but we don’t have enough middle-class housing.”

Despite his retirement, Hertzberg noted that he’s met with a handful of opposing groups, but states that many arguments against the initiative have not “done their homework.”

The League of Women Voters in California (LWV) declined to speak with RISMedia on the proposition, but they are opposed to it. The group’s argument is that the proposition essentially adds a second mortgage for buyers to repay, alongside their primary mortgage, each month.

“The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers,” the LWV’s voting recommendations state. “Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3% of the home price.”

The LWV also stated that voters would not know the interest rate, loan term or monthly payment amount prior to the program’s approval. Essentially, the LWV argues that the program would put homeowners in more debt.

Hertzberg rejected these notions, responding that the group’s arguments are “ridiculous” and that with purchase money security interest (PMSI), the only players to take a loss should there be a significant downturn in home prices are the banks and bondholders.

“PMSI means that there is no liability,” Hertzberg claims. “Assume we had a downturn, where a home’s value drops significantly. The bank and the bondholders take the loss. The only thing that the buyer loses if they buy a house for $900,000, is $30,000. There’s no downside risk beyond losing your down payment.”

He also emphasizes the safeguards the initiative includes, in reference to the 2008 financial crisis that rocked the world.

“People in 2008 had variable-rate mortgages. Their mortgage went from $1,200 to $2,400, and they couldn’t afford it. These down payment loans are fixed-rate mortgages. For renters, I promise you this much: In 10 years your rent’s going up. That doesn’t happen in a fixed-rate mortgage,” Hertzberg stresses.

While it may not be the optimal option for all first-time homebuyers, Garcia does acknowledge that some buyers in California may find use out of the program.

“I think it’s useful in a circumstance where a homebuyer or family has the income to cover the payments for both a first and second mortgage, but don’t have the liquidity,” he says. “It’s just an alternative pathway for individuals who just don’t have a lot of cash on hand to afford homeownership.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5624. Novee’s External Surface Testing checks which exposed assets attackers can actually exploit

Artificial intelligence penetration testing startup Novee Cyber Security Ltd. today added External Surface Testing to its platform so its AI-driven attacks can reach a customer’s entire internet-facing footprint.

External Surface Testing is aimed at the scramble after a critical vulnerability is disclosed, when security teams have to work out which exposed assets are affected and whether any can actually be exploited. Novee argues that attackers see a target as a single environment with many ways in, including forgotten subdomains and staging servers someone left exposed.

Conventional external attack surface management products catalog a company’s exposed assets and score them by severity. Netta Rager Dan, vice president of product at Novee, said those products “show you what’s exposed, but don’t give you the full picture of real risk.” In the company’s telling, security staff are left to validate long lists of exposures on their own.

Novee’s version needs nothing more than a domain name to get started. From there the software works outward the way an outside attacker would, and it keeps track of what it learns about each asset and service as it goes. A newly disclosed vulnerability gets run against a customer’s live systems to see whether anyone could actually exploit it.

Findings exported from other vendors’ attack surface tools go through the same check. Novee says the testing also catches flaws nobody had logged, chained attack paths among them, and the customer ends up with a short, prioritized list of validated issues backed by evidence.

Until now Novee’s testing has stopped at the application layer. External Surface Testing runs on the same platform as the company’s Application Pentesting product, so a host found during external discovery can be promoted straight into a full gray-box or white-box pentest. Whatever the discovery phase learned carries over. Novee claims no other fully autonomous AI pentesting platform covers the external attack surface as well as web, mobile and AI applications.

Limits are built in to keep the testing safe. Customers approve the scope before anything runs, and the probes come from outside the perimeter without agents or customer-supplied credentials. Exploit attempts don’t use destructive payloads. Traffic is held under configured caps so testing doesn’t cause load spikes or bury the security operations center in noise.

Former national-level offensive security operators Ido Geffen, Gon Chalamish and Omer Ninburg founded Novee in May 2025. YL Ventures LP, Canaan Partners and Zeev Ventures LP backed the company when it launched in January with $51.5 million in funding.

External Surface Testing is available now as part of the Novee platform.

#5623. Designer Ken Fulk Finds a Buyer for Midcentury Modern San Francisco ‘Tree House’—as Fully-Furnished Napa Valley Ranch Remains Up For Grabs

Celebrity designer Ken Fulk has found a buyer for his iconic San Francisco home, just two weeks after listing the property.

The Clarendon Heights abode is called the Duncan House, but Fulk lovingly named it the “Tree House." Although he told Realtor.com® he could not disclose details of the sale price, reports say the home was sold for $9,995,000—more than $2 million over the $7.9 million listing price.

Fulk and his husband, classical pianist Kurt Wootton, snapped up the property for $1.9 million in December 2010, according to The Real Deal. The couple scored the property at a discount, as the home was initially priced at $2.3 million that September.

The midcentury modern home was commissioned in 1959 and designed by Bay Area architect Charles Warren Callister.

"We are deeply honored to have been the stewards of that magnificent house for 16 years," Fulk told Realtor.com. "The next owner shares that same commitment. Meanwhile, we are tremendously excited to be moving into the heart of The City on a different hilltop."

“Hidden in the trees at one of the highest peaks in San Francisco, this midcentury architectural gem had been virtually untouched when Fulk purchased it and embarked on a respectful and lighthanded renovation,” a description on Fulk’s website reads.

“Leaving alone the soaring windows, the barrel-vaulted ceilings and the quirky layout, the amenities were modernized and the finishes were revitalized for a timeworn effect,” it continued. “Today, an otherworldly garden inspired by a Japanese hunting lodge surrounded the house.”

Fulk shared a tour of the stunning home with influencer Caleb Simpson, during which he explained that “the house only has two modes: It’s either a party palace or a temple.”

He also explained that the “whole house is made out of redwood,” but that the material is unfinished.

Adding that the wood requires quite a bit of maintenance, he even joked that when Wootton touches a surface after using hand lotion, it leaves a mark, and Fulk will quickly follow up with sandpaper to resolve it.

Still, the home has been thoroughly cared for since it was built, with Fulk claiming “every doorknob, every appliance, every tile” was in “pristine, original condition.”

Brilliantly decorated with all kinds of unique pieces—from a taxidermy giraffe mounted above the fireplace to an open-flame grill in the kitchen—the property is truly one-of-a-kind.

There's even a bedroom that's been completely converted into a dressing room, where racks of designer suits are carefully protected in garment bags with identifiable Polaroid photos displayed on the outside. Perfectly folded shirts are organized by color in pristine glass drawers, as is an extensive shoe collection.

In an Oct. 19 Instagram caption, Fulk opened up about the decision to leave the three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom dwelling he and his husband had called home for 16 years.

“So many things happening all at once! Kurt and I have made the big decision to leave our beloved Tree House high on the hill and move into the heart of the city,” he wrote. “We can’t wait to be more ingrained in the day to day life of this magical town.”

The designer shared a final look at the home in a Nov. 1 Instagram post.

"I took one last moment to soak it all in before entrusting this magical place to its next steward, who will love and care for it as we have," he captioned the post. "While we are tremendously excited for our next San Francisco adventure atop a different hill, we know there will never be another Tree House. Our hearts are full of gratitude, and our lives are all the richer for having spent these years beneath its magnificent roof."

In a comment on the post, Fulk confirmed that the couple will be relocating to Nob Hill, a historic neighborhood in San Francisco.

Fulk also noted that he is excited to be able to “ride the cable car” to his “new” flagship San Francisco studio. While the exact location has yet to be confirmed, it’s been reported that the new Ken Fulk location will be in Jackson Square and is expected to open in April 2027.

His previous headquarters—the “Magic Factory” in San Francisco’s SOMA district—was sold for $6 million in August of this year. The final sale price was under the initial asking price of $8.9 million. Fulk purchased the property in 2007 for $3 million.

Fulk also added that the couple’s five dogs will “spend most of their California time in the Napa Valley” but will occasionally visit the city.

“The idea of more country time for the dogs and more city for us feels like the perfect mix,” he added.

Currently, Fulk has another personal property on the market: a Napa Valley retreat on 76 private acres in Saint Helena, CA.

Fulk’s website describes Durham Ranch as his “beloved Napa Weekend escape” and the couple’s “satellite studio in the country,” noting that it’s been used as the “site of creative retreats, quiet weekends, and big celebrations.”

The home was listed for $4.5 million in July, and includes two bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms. It will be sold fully furnished, according to Galerie Magazine.

Fulk and Wootton bought the property in 2005 when it was in rough condition, and named it after their first golden retriever. Over time, it was transformed into a thoughtfully designed sanctuary with reclaimed materials and vintage finds.

The couple also own a waterfront estate in Provincetown, MA, and a Tribeca loft in New York City, which serves as a space to live as well as work.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5622. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5621. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5620. Chris Pratt Says He Was ‘Living in a Van’ With ‘About $60’ Before Big Hollywood Break

“Guardians of the Galaxy” actor Chris Pratt may be enjoying a lavish life as a movie star these days—but before he achieved major success in Hollywood, he was a restaurant server living humbly in Hawaii.

In an Oct. 29 post shared on X, the “Jurassic World” actor, 47, opened up about the unlikely encounter that turned it all around.

“Before Hollywood, I was living in a van in Hawaii and waiting tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp Company. One day, the incredible Rae Dawn Chong walked into the restaurant, and naturally, I went up to her table and said, ‘Hey, you’re a movie star! What are you doing here?’” he wrote.

When Chong, who starred in “The Color Purple,” asked Pratt if he could act, he recalled replying, “F-ck yeah, put me in your movie!”

From there, Chong asked for Pratt’s phone number.

“The only problem was I didn’t have one,” he said. “So I gave her my buddy Mike’s number instead.”

Pratt explained that “a couple days later,” his friend “casually” mentioned that someone had called looking for him. Pratt returned Chong’s call and discovered that her offer was legitimate.

“I drove over to pick up the script, went back to Mike’s house, and read all 120 pages three times in a row,” Pratt wrote, sharing that it was the first script he’d ever read. “My character’s name was Devon, and I remember thinking, ‘Sweet! I could totally play a Devon!’”

The father of four prepared extensively for the audition, which worked well in his favor.

“Rae told me I could act and offered me the part. I asked if we were shooting in Hawaii. Nope. Los Angeles,” he wrote.

With just “about $60” to his name, “a bag of clothes, and some rollerblades,” Pratt sensed his situation would be changing soon.

“Then Rae told me they’d fly me out. And I remember thinking right then and there, my life just changed forever,” he wrote. “I’m going to be an actor.”

Pratt remarked he will “forever be grateful to Rae for taking a chance on a kid working at a shrimp restaurant,” adding that the “little movie” that gave him his start was the 2000 film “Cursed: Part III”—a project he described as “a low-budget horror comedy. That opened the door to Hollywood for me.”

The actor’s living arrangements have been given quite the upgrade in the years since he was staying in a van.

Pratt and his wife, Katherine Schwarzenegger, 36, are reportedly residing in a Montecito property that was previously home to pop star Katy Perry as they try to offload their sprawling Pacific Palisades mansion.

The couple has been trying to sell for years, after purchasing the property in June 2018 for $15.6 million and razing the existing home to build the custom 13,000-square-foot megamansion that currently stands.

The price has been slashed a few times since they initially listed it for $32 million in July 2023, and it currently sits at $19.99 million—the lowest price it has been, in its fifth time on the market in three years.

The listing, which is held by Shana Tavangarian of Carolwood Estates, describes the six-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom abode as a “one of a kind architectural masterpiece” that was created “with no expense spared.”

Boasting “luxury quality construction” and “grand scale and volume throughout,” the estate is located on just under an acre within a “boutique gated community”

While it was initially understood that the property had been intended to serve as the couple's permanent family home, they ended up purchasing another mansion for $12.5 million in 2023, this time opting for a parcel that is just a stone's throw from the Brentwood house of Schwarzenegger's mother, Maria Shriver.

Again, they demolished the dwelling that stood on that parcel in order to begin construction on another custom manse, which they broke ground on in 2024.

Their most recent construction project has already sparked furious controversy, however, after it was revealed that Pratt and Schwarzenegger had demolished a midcentury modern property designed by acclaimed architect Craig Ellwood in order to make way for their new custom dwelling.

Design fans were upset by the couple's decision to tear down the original structure, known as the Zimmerman House, which dated to the 1950s and was considered a design gem.

Work on that property is still understood to be ongoing—and it appears that, while they wait for their latest home to be completed, Pratt and Schwarzenegger are continuing to reside in the Montecito property once owned by Perry and her former fiancé, Orlando Bloom.

#5619. Groundcover turns its Wand acquisition into a Kubernetes rightsizing beta

Observability company groundcover Inc. today added Autonomous Infrastructure to its platform in beta to rightsize the processor and memory requests automatically on customers’ Kubernetes workloads based on how each workload behaves in production.

The technology comes from Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd., which groundcover acquired in September.

The release is aimed at the processor and memory requests Kubernetes has engineers set for each workload up front, usually before it has handled any real traffic, and groundcover said most teams seldom return to those numbers. When one is set too low, the first sign is often a service throwing out-of-memory errors. Padding that goes unused ends up on the monthly cloud bill.

Because the groundcover sensor has been collecting production history all along, a customer on a supported version can open Autonomous Infrastructure for the first time without installing anything and find the data the feature needs already in place. Requested processor and memory for each workload appear next to actual usage. Estimated monthly savings sit beside a count of under-provisioned workloads, and a chart tracks over time how much of the potential saving has been realized.

Dollar figures in the beta are based on a price per processor and memory unit that customers enter themselves. Public cloud pricing is the next step, according to groundcover, and billing data such as the Cost and Usage Report from Amazon Web Services Inc. will come after that.

Most resource optimization tools size each workload in isolation, groundcover argues, so a request that looks right for one service can still starve its neighbors on a crowded node. Stability is the first constraint in groundcover’s own software. Before Autonomous Infrastructure raises a request, it checks how tightly the node is already packed so one workload’s increase does not leave the rest short of resources.

Shahar Azulay, groundcover’s co-founder and chief executive, said customers can check what their clusters stand to save, from data already held in their own cloud accounts, before they let Autonomous Infrastructure “change anything.” The feature stays off until an engineer turns it on and picks the deployments, namespaces or clusters it manages.

During the beta the software touches requests only and leaves limits where they are. Each policy carries minimum and maximum bounds for processor and memory, and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. Groundcover suggests starting with lower-risk workloads such as development namespaces and leaving alone something like a production database that needs room to grow.

The beta is available now at no additional cost to every groundcover customer running its sensor on Kubernetes, and the company is also recruiting design partners to work with its product team while it runs. Demonstrations are scheduled for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City Nov. 9-12.

Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

#5618. Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

#5617. Offerpad CEO: Market Issues Main Cause of Glum Q3 Performance

In a Q3 2026 earnings report Nov. 2, iBuyer Offerpad, known for giving homeowners cash offers within 24 hours, blamed the less-than-stout housing market for its less-than-stout numbers.

In a release and press conference, the company reported a net loss of $11.5 million, or $2.30 a share—with total closed real estate transactions numbering 324. Gross profit was $6.5 million, with a gross margin of 8.3%. Contribution profit after interest per real estate transaction was approximately $12,900, near Q2 levels and about double the prior-year quarter.

On the plus side, the 324 real estate transactions were up from 295 in the second quarter and 263 in the first quarter, marking a steady sequential recovery in activity.

Brian Bair, Offerpad’s chairman and CEO, explained that high mortgage rates and slowing buyer demand were the main culprits for the lackluster Q3 performance.

“Mortgage rates rose more than 70 basis points from mid-August to early October, putting additional pressure on housing affordability and slowing buyer demand,” he said. “As homes took longer to sell, we adjusted our acquisition criteria to require higher expected returns and became more selective about new purchases, while serving more sellers through Cash Offer Marketplace and Brokerage Services. Having multiple ways to serve homeowners gives us flexibility to keep growing transactions while maintaining capital discipline.”

“Our focus is converting inventory into cash and continuing to optimize our cost base,” added Andrew Pieper, interim CFO. “Together, we expect those actions to continue to support liquidity and lower the transaction volume required to reach Adjusted EBITDA breakeven.”

Offerpad shares closed the regular session at $2.07, down 4.61% from the previous close of $2.17. In after-hours trading, the stock dipped to $2.05, down 0.97% from the close. From the prior day’s close to the after-hours quote, the shares were down around 5.5%. The stock is trading near the low end of its 52-week range of $2.06 to $26.70, showing how far investor sentiment has weakened over the past year.

Questioned after the formal conference about the current home seller mentality, Bair noted that it has for sure changed.

“We have seen this thing evolve over the last several years, but I think this is the very first time that a majority of the sellers know it is a buyer’s market,” he said. “They are seeing active listings around their areas continue to increase. The good part about that is that we can buy at wider margins and be more selective about what we are acquiring.

“Of course, what we have to be very sensitive to is making sure that we are buying the right type of product in the right areas. We are continuing to stick with the interior homes. The outlying areas are definitely impacted more than most areas. Our portfolio still consists of interior homes, newer, not as much renovation. Of course, we still have renovation, but the $100,000 renovation projects that we have done in the past, we are not looking at doing right now.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5616. San Diego Accountant Tricked Investors Into Sinking $8.2 Million Into Phony ADU Venture

A California man convinced dozens of investors to pour millions of dollars into a real estate venture he claimed would deliver big returns through the construction of backyard homes.

But the 30-year-old accountant lost more than $8.2 million of their money in risky stock market trades and not a single accessory dwelling unit (ADU) was built, prosecutors said.

Ethan Joseph Sanchez, of San Diego, was sentenced to 63 months in federal prison after admitting to orchestrating the investment fraud scheme, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of California announced Friday.

“Ethan Sanchez exploited the trust of hardworking people and stole their savings through lies and fabricated investments,” U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon said in a statement. “This sentence reflects the profound harm he caused.”

Sanchez, who was a certified public accountant at the time and operated through his business, BSC Equity Ventures LLC., repeatedly lied to his victims as to how their investment funds would be used, according to prosecutors.

The scheme began back in 2022 when Sanchez allegedly began soliciting loans from investors, falsely claiming the money would fund real estate ventures, including the construction and renovation of ADUs.

He promised the investors they would receive their principal back as soon as possible, with an above-average return of interest, in some cases as much as 25%.

Sanchez also allegedly used a fictitious identity, Richard “Rick” Aguilar, to make the investment opportunities appear more legitimate.

But prosecutors say Sanchez used the investors’ funds for day trading and in most cases lost the money. He did not fund the real estate transactions he said the investors were financing nor did he build any of the ADUs he said would be financed with the investors’ money.

The FBI reported in February 2025 that BSC Equity Ventures had received over $6 million in investments from its investors, while Sanchez returned less than $1.8 million to them.

At the sentencing hearing on Oct. 30, U.S. District Judge Robert S. Huie ordered Sanchez to forfeit over $8.2 million and to pay restitution to victims.

He described the scheme as “aggravated and reprehensible,” highlighting how Sanchez had used existing victims to recruit additional investors, sometimes including members of their own families.

The judge described the harm caused by the scheme as “almost unimaginable,” adding that the consequences went far beyond the financial losses.

In a January 2026 interview with ABC 10News, one investor, identified only as Brooke, said the loss he suffered forced him out of retirement and back to work to rebuild his savings.

Brooke told the outlet that Sanchez told him he needed money to refinance his portfolio of investment properties and would pay interest on the loans. Sanchez initially borrowed $40,000 from Brooke in December 2023, but then continued to borrow more money, including a $150,000 loan.

Sanchez made small payments, Brooke said, but never repaid the full amount of his investment. Brooke also said that he had borrowed against his home to make the investment with Sanchez and was paying interest on that money.

“It was always lie after lie,” he said. “And then it became so obvious that this was a Ponzi scheme.”

#5613. Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools

Snowflake Inc. today announced a sweeping collection of artificial intelligence capabilities designed to bring business context, governance and autonomous development into the same environment, as enterprises increasingly hand over software engineering and everyday operations to AI agents.

The announcements, during the company’s Expedition 2026 virtual conference, include a new Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering capabilities that allow AI agents to build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention.

The company is betting that more coders and engineers will use AI throughout the software development lifecycle as creation moves even faster, while other back-end departments begin to adopt agents in their day-to-day work. For example, sales operations are creating agents that can analyze sales risks and prepare customer outreach without writing code.

“AI is industrializing software creation. Actually, it’s industrializing intelligence,” Chief Executive Sridhar Ramaswamy said. “What once took months can now take hours, days, or even minutes.”

Ramaswamy noted that while AI is changing the economics of software development, as agents take over tasks usually relegated to specialized developers, business users become developers. This is changing the competitive landscape, meaning that the advantage no longer goes to specialists, but to proprietary knowledge.

Snowflake is taking the field by helping ordinary AI models understand and contextualize that business knowledge. It does this with Business Ontology, an extension of its existing semantic views that lets organizations establish approved definitions used across the organization. Without a standard definition, two agents could respond to the same business-related question with incompatible answers, even when both agents have accurate underlying data.

Using information from Business Ontology, Snowflake CoCo, the coding agent for data teams, and Snowflake CoWork, the personal work agent for knowledge workers, use these approved business concepts to ground their responses.

This new feature is currently in private preview, but is headed to public preview soon.

Cortex AI Gateway arrives to become a single front door for agents within an organization. It is not entirely new; Snowflake introduced it in July 2026 as a centralized way to govern and monitor agents.

Today’s announcement expands its capabilities rather than introducing the gateway for the first time. The new updates include agent abuse detection, observability and tracing, Cortex sandboxes, AI cost governance, dynamic model routing and tools integration using technology from Snowflake’s Natoma acquisition.

“An agent that acts on your business has to be trusted, and it has to know three important things: what the data means, which data to trust, and what it’s allowed to do,” said Ramaswamy.

The platform most importantly applies existing security mechanisms, including data masking and access restrictions, to agent-driven operations while adding capabilities to monitor activity, detect potential abuse and maintain records of what agents do. The information technology and security teams can also apply cost controls, select models based on efficiency or accuracy and restrict which external tools agents can access granularly.

The underlying role of this governance, control and transparency is aligned with giving agents the same sort of role observation granted to employees. Treating them similarly in terms of autonomy.

Snowflake’s push comes amid a broader industry race to establish the control layer for enterprise AI agents. SAP has been expanding its Autonomous Enterprise architecture and governed Joule agents, while Salesforce has introduced its Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane to secure autonomous workflows. Snowflake is approaching the same problem from the data platform side, seeking to become the foundation through which agents access trusted business information and operate under enterprise policies.

Snowflake also announced the public preview of Cortex Training, which will allow customers to tailor open-weight AI models with their own proprietary information.

The service is designed to make it simpler to create specialized models using post-training without needing vast arrays of graphics processing units. Snowflake lets them train models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Specialized, smaller models that come with more efficient responses, faster responses, and frequently cost benefits in terms of tokens,” Executive Vice President of Product Christian Kleinerman said.

Many enterprise companies will require sovereign control of their own AI models as increasing restrictions on foreign open-weight AI or regulations on handling sensitive information. It’s easier to audit what passes through an AI model on your own hardware than in a third-party vendor’s cloud.

Separately, Snowflake announced an expanded partnership with Oracle Corp. to make its platform available as a first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The integration will give customers easier access to Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities while allowing them to work directly through Oracle databases and applications.

#5612. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

#5610. Court Report: NAR Fires Back in Compass Subpoena Spat; Keller Williams Sued for ‘Junk Fees’

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

NAR defends Compass subpoena in private listing lawsuit

The latest dust-up in the battle between now defunct PLS.com and the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) continues, as both parties await a judge’s decision on whether Compass can be compelled to provide witness and other evidence in the case.

Last week, a filing from NAR’s attorneys outlines the association’s opposition to a motion—by Compass, which is a non-party in the case—to quash subpoenas issued by NAR.

Within the memorandum, NAR argues that “Compass wants to supply PLS a friendly Compass witness while simultaneously, and blanketly, refusing to produce any documents for fair cross-examination. That hand-picked witness is Compass’s Chief Strategy Officer, Ashton Alexander.”

After significant back-and-forth, it appeared that NAR had dropped its demand to depose Compass CEO Robert Reffkin, but the two sides continue to wrangle over other witnesses—including rank-and-file Compass agents—as well as document requests that Compass has described as overly broad and “burdensome.”

“As outlined in our court filing, the petitioners cannot provide a witness to testify in support of PLS while simultaneously refusing to produce documents necessary for NAR to fairly cross-examine its witness,” an NAR spokesperson told RISMedia.

The association also argues that through various email threads, Reffkin and Alexander coordinated with PLS co-founder Mauricio Umansky in a “quest” against NAR’s Clear Cooperation Policy (CCP). PLS first sued NAR (and big MLSs) way back in 2020, settling with the MLSs and temporarily dropping the case against NAR before reviving it last year.

NAR’s court filings included emailed exchanges between Compass executives and Umansky over the last two years, including Reffkin sharing an op-ed slamming Clear Cooperation ahead of publication, and talking points on the policy ahead of both men attending an industry conference in early 2025.

In a joint filing from Compass and NAR, the brokerage argued that subpoenaing six non-party witnesses—including Reffkin, Alexander and Compass President of Integrated Services Cory Perkins—is “unduly burdensome on its face.”

NAR’s subpoenas focus on communications with clients and how those clients want to list their homes for sale, documents about membership in real estate trade association and other communications that Compass argues NAR should also possess.

So far, Compass stated that NAR is retaliating against Compass because one executive agreed to provide a deposition testimony for PLS.

NAR, on the other hand, argues that Alexander’s deposition and the documents it requested could implicate the testimony or documents of the other Compass-affiliated agents.

“The stakes are high,” NAR’s argument states.

The association’s explanations for the subpoenas also touch upon requests for further information from Compass, specifically information that PLS cannot provide.

“(The documents the parties themselves have produced) do not entail the Compass-affiliated agents’ listing agreements, which would reflect seller opt-outs of the MLS, or show whether off-MLS marketing was driven by seller preference or the agent’s business objectives. The bare listing information that PLS produced does not absolve Compass of its duties; PLS, for example, never tracked sales data,” NAR’s argument states.

Both parties, and Compass as a non-party, await a judge’s decision on whether the brokerage will have to provide the subpoenaed documents and communications.

Another player enters Compass MLS lawsuits

The Northern California-based MLS, MLSListings, announced that it has joined six MLSs in their federal lawsuit against Compass.

The six other MLSs in the lawsuit alongside MLSListings are Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service (ARMLS), BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS and REcolorado.

Two other MLSs—OneKey and CRMLS—are suing Compass in a separate but largely identical lawsuit. All of the MLS’ appeared to have received legal threats from Compass back in September, focused on listing restrictions.

According to the amended complaint, the lawsuit arises from a “campaign by Compass to pressure MLSs into changing cooperation rules in a way that would favor Compass but would make the market for residential real estate less transparent and less competitive, ultimately hurting consumers.”

“In Silicon Valley and throughout Northern California, buyers, sellers and real estate professionals depend on timely, accurate information to make important financial decisions,” MLSListings President and CEO Dave Wetzel said. “When publicly marketed homes are withheld from the shared marketplace, buyers lose access to opportunities, sellers may miss potential offers, and smaller brokerages are placed at a disadvantage. We are joining this lawsuit to defend the cooperation that gives everyone a fair opportunity to compete and helps consumers make informed decisions.”

Although the case is still ongoing and has just begun, the results of the lawsuit could change how brokerages list their properties on MLS databases. The amended complaint argues that Compass “wants to have its cake and eat it too,” where the brokerage may benefit from listings provided by other brokerages onto each MLS, without having to add their own listings into the database.

Initially, ARMLS and its fellow organizations filed the lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 21, after California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS) filed its initial complaint against the brokerage a few weeks prior.

MLSListing’s participation in the lawsuit adds another name to Compass’s list of disgruntled MLSs. The New York-based MLS, OneKey® MLS, had also joined CRMLS as a plaintiff in its federal lawsuit against Compass last week.

Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison

The affluential luxury real estate brokers, Tal and Oren Alexander, along with their brother Alon were sentenced to 30 years in federal prison last week.

Earlier in March, the brothers were found guilty on all charges of rape and sex-trafficking, after several named and unnamed women came forward and shared their stories.

One victim, under the pseudonym Isa Brooks, stated that she was just 16 years old when two of the brothers and their friend had raped her.

“I cry for the innocence of that terrified 16-year-old and stand for her today,” Brooks said, reported by CNN. “Their eyes went black. As if I was being mauled by animals.”

“I grieve the girl that I was,” she said.

The case began toward the end of 2024, where the brothers were arrested on charges of operating “a long-running sex trafficking scheme, as part of which they raped and sexually assaulted women to whom they had provided ‘material benefits,’ including domestic and international travel to vacation destinations, luxury accommodations at high-end hotels and vacation properties, and access to other luxury experiences and events,” according to a filed indictment.

Within the court proceedings, Judge Valerie Caproni showed little mercy for the brothers, who continued to claim their innocence to the charges throughout the sentencing process.

“Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives. It has caused long lasting damage to them. Many have significant problems trusting people,” Caproni said, reported by CNN.

Despite several letters written to Caproni by friends and family of the Alexander brothers, Caproni once again reprimanded the trio for their crimes and their conduct.

“You did not have to stand up and say you’ve never raped anyone,” Caproni said, according to ABC News. “That’s a lie and you know it.”

Zillow pays out over $210 million to settle shareholders

After nearly five years of court proceedings, a settlement was reached in Jaeger v. Zillow Group litigation, in which shareholders argued that the portal did not adequately disclose its struggles to ramp up its now-defunct iBuying business, and misled investors.

Last Wednesday, Zillow announced that it would pay out over $212.5 million to the shareholders, who claimed that the portal had misrepresented the success of “Zillow Offers,” and failed to accurately disclose struggles it faced in flipping homes.

Both Zillow and Hagens Berman—the plaintiff’s attorneys for the case—have stated that they are satisfied with the settlement and await a judge’s approval.

“We are incredibly pleased to obtain this result for investors,” said Steve Berman, managing partner of Hagens Berman.

In a statement shared with RISMedia, a Zillow spokesperson commented, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

According to a regulatory filing from Zillow, about $48 million of the settlement will be paid through insurance proceeds. Hagens Berman said in a statement the settlement was “potentially the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington federal court.”

Prior to the settlement, the case was slated to reach trial in September 2027.

The case began with Zillow’s iBuying business, also known as Zillow Offers, which was launched in spring 2018. Zillow Offers was a house flipping initiative, where the company promised that it could scale the business model of buying and quickly flipping homes using technology to predict short-term market fluctuations and patterns.

Zillow Offers was shut down later in 2021, and sold a backlog of nearly 18,000 homes at a loss of about $550 million. Within the original complaint, Hagens Berman argued that several statements and communications from Zillow were “materially false and/or misleading” and had failed to disclose “material adverse facts” about Zillow’s business, operations and prospects.

Homebuyer sues Keller Williams over $650 “junk fee”

Broker fees are once again on the receiving end of litigation, as one homebuyer in Pennsylvania filed a complaint—consisting of over 30 pages—against Keller Williams Elite in Lancaster County’s Court of Common Pleas.

According to the complaint, Gregory Deivert, a recent buyer client, is suing the franchise over a $650 fee that he claims is essentially for nothing.

“The fee had no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it. It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for him,” the complaint states.

A final settlement statement was included in the filing, and the complaint references the breakdown of fees within the statement. Deivert’s attorney argues that the $650 broker fee is a prototypical “junk fee,” and that Keller Williams Elite was fully compensated for its services by the $14,700 commission it received from the seller.

The issue of “junk fees” is nothing new to the real estate industry. In 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) launched a formal inquiry into the issue of extra fees tacked onto home mortgage costs.

Generally, the complaint argues that customarily, broker fees are paid for by the seller and are included in the broker’s commission. Within the lawsuit, Deivert is suing the brokerage for a breach of fiduciary duty and a violation of the Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law.

As for relief, Deivert is asking for $50,000 from the brokerage, along with a declaration that Keller Williams Elite will be prohibited from charging the $650 fee again, and labeling it as a fixed fee for broker compensation without disclosing what it entails.

#5609. 10-Acre Florida Ranch With NBA-Level Facility Is Listed for $38.9 Million in Celebrity Enclave Where Gisele Bündchen Lives

An enormous 9.69-acre Florida compound with a brand-new 10,500-square-foot entertainment facility "that can be transformed into anything you can imagine" and resort-inspired grounds has just hit the market in Southwest Ranches for an astonishing $38.9 million.

If it reels in anywhere near its asking price, the 23,442-square-foot estate could become one of the top sales in the ultrahigh net worth neighborhood that celebrities, professional athletes, and supermodel Gisele Bündchen call home.

"I have never seen a property done to this scale before," says Tommy Crivello of the Tommy Crivello Real Estate Group, who is co-listing the property with Angeline Earnest of Coldwell Banker Realty.

Once the home of Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, the luxury residence last traded hands for $9,000,000 in 2022. Its asking price of $1,659 per square foot is currently the highest-priced listing in the exclusive Sunshine Ranches enclave of Southwest Ranches.

"Everything has been completely redone with extensive remodeling," Earnest notes. "The landscaping, garage, pools, and the 10,000-square-foot recreational facility are all new. Every structure also has a new roof."

The sprawling property boasts a five-bedroom primary residence, a three-bedroom guesthouse with a catering-grade kitchen, a members-style clubhouse with a full bar and private theater, and a gym and spa wellness retreat with a massage room and cold plunge.

Private lakes, immersive art, koi ponds, "producing orchards," a Tiki pavilion, and two pools, including one with a custom 10-foot rock-jumping wall, can also be found on the enormous lot. An outdoor basketball court and hockey rink round out the property.

"There are 10 acres of walkable space," she adds. "It feels like the whole property is livable and is not overwhelming."

"We are seeing a lot of high-end celebrities coming here," Crivello says. "I see an entrepreneur, hedge fund person, athlete, or real big car collector buying this property. It could also be someone who is looking for a place for the entire family, as it is designed for multigenerational living."

A custom-engineered lighting system transforms the pathways into nocturnal works of art. For equestrians, the sale also includes plans for a seven-stall barn with oversized paddocks.

"The property is large enough that there is room for another outdoor facility, and it has direct access to miles of riding trails," he says. "Everything in Southwest Ranches has rural zoning, so you can have a garden and any kind of animal on property. It just flows effortlessly."

Created as a "fully integrated private campus," the serene property also features art installations and curated gathering spaces for entertaining.

“You can get to the beach in 30 minutes, Amerant Bank Arena in 15 minutes, Las Olas Boulevard for the nightlife, and Pembroke Gardens is just 10 minutes away,” Crivello says. “You can retreat to the country, or you can be in the limelight as much as you want to be.”

Built in 1964, the Chicago brick-clad main estate boasts a renovated interior with two guest suites, each with a private entrance and that “function as private apartments within the residence.”

A lavish upstairs primary wing has a breakfast bar, a refrigerator, a seating area, dual bathrooms, separate closets, and a private terrace.

Other highlights include an executive office, a chef’s kitchen, a built-in wine preservation system, a custom bar, and a wraparound covered balcony on the main level.

A detached garage pavilion spanning nearly 2,000 square feet is fully air-conditioned. The four-vehicle structure has lift capability to accommodate up to eight vehicles. It also has floor drains, integrated compressor and vacuum systems, EV-ready outlets, workstation walls, and extra storage space.

One of the most impressive features of the property is its enormous entertainment facility, “currently home to a nonprofit basketball program.”

The “NBA-level” structure features professional athletic flooring, locker rooms, conference spaces, a viewing balcony, and a smoothie bar.

Its flexible design could also be reimagined into a 50- to 100-vehicle auto showroom, a private museum, a production studio, or an event venue.

“The nice thing about the facility is that it has a second mezzanine where you can have spectators watch,” Crivello notes.

“You could also transform it into an indoor equestrian facility. It offers the peace of mind that upscale riders want. There has been a big shift for people who are car collectors, so the facility could also be transformed into an auto showroom. The building is huge and would be a focal point for an equestrian, athlete, or car collector.”
