#5592. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5591. Florida Voters Approve Landmark Measure To Reform Property Taxes

Florida voters are projected to approve a measure that would reform the state's property tax system, increasing the homestead property tax exemption and reducing the tax bill for some households.

Amendment 3, championed by outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, aims to increase the homestead property tax exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and raise it again to $250,000 in 2028. DeSantis estimated the latter threshold would eliminate property tax for 60% of Florida homeowners.

At 9:45 p.m. ET, with 98% of votes reported, the Associated Press reported the measure had 62% of votes in favor and 38% opposed. The measure, which would go into effect in 2027, needs 60% voter approval to pass.

"Big win on Amendment 3 for Florida homeowners!," DeSantis posted to X.

The exemption would only apply to Floridians who established residency prior to December 2026. New residents would need to wait five years before being eligible for the exemptions.

The measure would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties to 5%, down from the current 10%.

Byron Donalds, a GOP representative projected to win the election to replace the term-limited DeSantis, supported the measure. His opponent, Democrat David Jolly, did not. AP projects that Donalds will win the governor's race.

"In a state where homeowners insurance premiums are growing quickly due to climate concerns, which in turn drives HOA dues higher as well, any relief from the annual carrying costs of owning a home in Florida is welcome," says Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner.

Berner notes that the median listing price in Florida fell 3.5% year over year in September and the number of homes for sale fell 9.6% from last year.

"Buyers and sellers are opting out of participation in the market as affordability constraints keep deals from going the distance at prices both parties can agree upon," the economist says.

On Tuesday night, Florida Realtors® President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said the result proved "Florida homeowners chose property tax relief".

"At a time when families are paying more for housing, insurance, groceries and everyday necessities, voters seized the opportunity to keep more of their own hard-earned money, taking a meaningful step toward making Florida a more affordable place to buy, own and keep a home," he said in a statement to Realtor.com.

"Florida Realtors was proud to stand with homeowners in supporting Amendment 3. We have worked with state and local leaders for decades to reduce barriers to homeownership, and we look forward to building on that partnership as Florida puts this relief into place responsibly, without compromising the essential services our communities depend on.”

The MidFlorida Credit Union estimated in 2024 that the average homeowner in the state pays around $2,338 a year in property taxes. In more expensive areas like Miami-Dade County or Palm Beach County, taxes can be significantly higher.

DeSantis argued that the measure would provide much-needed financial relief for homeowners. Opponents argued the reduction in property tax revenue would have a deleterious effect on local governments.

Florida does not have an individual income tax or estate taxes, creating a limited pool of money for local governments to fund with. State economists had argued that the measure would wipe out nearly a quarter of all funding for local governments and deprive schools of billions in local revenue, hitting smaller counties especially hard.

In August, a circuit court judge ruled that the bill's original title, "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes" was "clearly and conclusively defective" and "more akin to a political slogan" than a neutral statement. The judge also dinged the bill for including "factually inaccurate" language and ordered that ballot language be amended prior to the midterm election.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier then changed the name of the proposed amendment to the "Homestead Tax Exemptions, Property Assessments, and Spending Restrictions Amendment" and revised the language that ultimately appeared on the ballot.

A model by NAR found cutting property taxes by $200 a month lowered the income needed to afford the median-priced Florida home from about $133,800 to $125,200—a move that would put roughly 242,000 additional households above the affordability threshold. Among households under 45, NAR estimates about 93,500 more could afford a starter home, including roughly 40,000 younger renters.

Florida homeowners might be thinking of more immediate relief, though. The state has some of the highest homeowners association fees in the country. It is also a center of the nation's property insurance crisis.

Florida Realtors' political action committee put $18 million into a "Vote Yes on 3" campaign, according to WPTV, significantly out-raising its opponents. In a previously published op-ed to Realtor.com, Bonfiglio Jr. denied that the measure necessarily meant cuts to public services.

“Voting yes on Amendment 3 is Step 1, where Floridians decide that homeowners deserve this relief. But we can't forget about Step 2: implementation, where communities will work through how to deliver that relief while keeping public safety and core services first,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, opponents argue that such a measure would increase costs for public services, and that the measure privileges the desires of homeowners over non-homeowning citizens. An analysis published by the Florida Housing Coalition found that an estimated $1.61 billion in property taxes could be shifted to rental homes in 2028, growing to $2.19 billion by 2031.

"There's a small segment of homeowners that will benefit from this," Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator, told NPR. "But the majority of people — renters, business owners, everyone else, and even many homeowners — won't see any benefit from this amendment at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5590. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5589. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5588. Tennessee Voters Opt To Ban State-Level Property Taxes

Voters in Tennessee are projected to approve Amendment 2, which bans any future statewide property tax and enshrines the prohibition in the state constitution.

Tennessee has not had a statewide property tax since 1949, though the state Legislature technically retained the constitutional authority to create one. Instead, property taxes are levied at the local level.

At 11 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the measure had 66.4% support with 82% of votes reporting, according to The Associated Press. An amendment to the Tennessee Constitution passes if it gets at least 50% support, and the number of “yes” votes is more than half of all votes cast for governor.

"It ensures that the state cannot impose property taxes again, putting taxpayers’ interests first and reinforcing local control," said Republican state Rep. Tandy Darby, who sponsored the amendment.

Amendment 2 would not prevent counties and municipal authorities from levying property taxes, but would prohibit the General Assembly from issuing property taxes now and in the future.

In order to change that, the state constitution would have to be amended once more, which would require a two-thirds vote in two legislative sessions and voter approval.

Republican Gov. Bill Lee came out in support of the initiative. It's supported by the National Federation of Independent Business as well as the Tennessee Realtors®.

Conservative nonprofit Tennessee Stands said the amendment "reinforces the principle that private property rights should never be subject to excessive government taxation or the threat of confiscation."

Some Democrats have opposed it on the grounds that the ban does not need to be written into the constitution and should remain a state statute.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5587. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5586. Realtors Predict These Nine Cities Will Be Unaffordable by 2027

Vibrant-Colored neon lights on a busy night at the bars and honky-tonks in the country music center, Broadway, the tourism center of Downtown Nashville, Tennessee

(TNS)–Home prices are climbing across the nation and some markets are hotter than others. According to a new report from Finance Buzz, nine U.S. cities are likely to become unaffordable by 2027, due to an influx of out-of-town buyers and tight inventory.

Here’s a look at the popular locales where housing costs are outpacing local incomes, as per Finance Buzz’s reporting:

Many areas in northern New Jersey are popular for people relocating out of New York City.

According to Daniel Smith, team lead at Smith Realty Team, homes in Montclair are expected to stay in high demand and continue commanding higher home prices.

“Retirees and pre-retirees are also targeting these towns because of their vibrant downtowns, access to health care, and cultural amenities, which makes competition even stronger,” he said.

Nashville attracted numerous new residents during the pandemic years, offering a lively city experience alongside lower taxes and a more affordable cost of living.

While home prices have come down slightly over the past year, the median sale price is currently $464,983 and real estate experts don’t expect a reduction any time soon.

Realtor Carla Gericke, with Porcupine Real Estate, said that “no income tax, easy access to Boston, and that elusive small-town feel with real community bones” is causing Nashua’s popularity to spike.

“Nashua’s median home price has soared to the $500,000 to $550,000 range, and demand keeps outpacing supply,” she said.

Gericke urged retirees looking to buy in the state to act quickly or venture outside the bigger cities to find better deals.

Arizona has long been a top destination for retirees hoping to escape the cold. Fred Loguidice, a real estate expert and founder of several home-buying companies in the area, said that home demand is outpacing supply, making it a market that is likely to stay competitive in the future.

“In markets like Phoenix, fewer homes are being built while demand persists, so prices consistently escalate,” he said.

Real estate expert Fred Loguidice also highlighted demand for Northeast hubs like the Buffalo metro area. While Zillow put the median home price at a moderate $261,300, home values in the area have been increasing.

“That momentum is a hard habit to break,” he said, noting its affordability and surging job opportunities make it a top choice for relocation for people in the region and beyond.

Athens is about 60 miles northeast of Atlanta and attracts many buyers and visitors alike with its lively college town atmosphere, excellent dining scene, and more.

While Georgia is often cited as a top spot to retire, thanks to the weather and lower cost of living, real estate trends indicate that home prices will continue to climb throughout the next year or so. Prices have gone up over the past year, with the median currently sitting at $353,333.

Florida boasts many affordable cities and tax incentives for retirees, but those considering Tampa may want to reassess.

Omer Reiner, realtor and president of Florida Cash Home Buyers, said home prices in the city are already high, and rising insurance costs are putting many popular areas out of reach.

“This is especially true for those nearing or at retirement, as higher costs of living when you are on any type of fixed income means you are spending more for less,” he said.

Iowa isn’t particularly known for its excessive home prices, but demand has been on the rise in Des Moines, according to real estate investor Jacob Naig, particularly for homes popular with retirees.

“Single-family homes, as well as small multi-family properties and single-level ranch-style homes that are particularly desirable to aging buyers, have seen a substantial rise in demand,” he said.

Many cities in the Pacific Northwest have seen rapidly rising home prices, and Ontario, which sits on the border of Oregon and Idaho, is no different. With stunning desert views, mountain ranges, and more, it’s a haven for outdoorsy types.

But recent real estate trends indicated it could be unaffordable in the coming years. Average home prices have risen steadily over the past year and currently sit at $307,769.

#5585. Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation

Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees.

Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company.

In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later.

Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July. Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease.

Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc.

Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor.

Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia Capital. That Series E round raised $350 million at an $8 billion valuation, per Bloomberg, and fal said the two rounds come to $1.65 billion combined. Last December, the company raised $140 million at a $4.5 billion valuation.

Investors have now put more than $1.9 billion into the company.

#5584. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5583. Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem

For buyers, especially first-time buyers, today’s housing affordability crisis (driven by a host of market challenges, from rising mortgage rates to low inventory and lingering inflation) creates many barriers to entry for homeownership. Is there anything agents can actually do at the local level to move the needle and help their clients achieve their homeownership goals?

Four brokerage leaders recently gathered at RISMedia 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange on a panel titled, “Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem,” to say yes and share their tactics and long-term solutions for buyers facing today’s housing affordability problem.

The session, moderated by RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, included panelists Keith Smith, co-owner, Yes Realty Partners, a Keller Williams Alliance Partner; Ennis Antoine, owner and CEO, EA Realty of Georgia; Katey McGrath, vice president, director of operations, Elfant Wissahickon Realtors®; and Ken Baris, CEO, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Jordan Baris Realty.

Here’s a glimpse into some of the questions and answers that provided attendees with some detailed takeaways to help their clients overcome the affordability challenge.

John Featherston: To set the stage, tell us why brokers should care about the housing affordability issue?

Keith Smith: I’m just going to kind of say the awkward thing to the room. Every single one of us makes a living either directly or indirectly from helping people buy and sell. And if we can’t help people buy and sell, we’re not going to be able to put our key in the door. We’re not going to be able to begin our business. Right now, first-time homebuyers can’t buy, and they’re 40? You have Boomers who will not be able to move on. So if we can’t help people do that, this isn’t just a certain entry point. It’s all the way across the board. I think maybe a little bit later we’ll talk about some possible solutions.

Katey McGrath: Obviously it’s good business. And what’s interesting too is at least in our market, the competition for that business is a lot less intense because it is a little bit more work and it’s not as dollar-productive. It’s absolutely more rewarding and more valuable to your communities, but not everybody gets up and says, “I want to sell lower-priced houses.” And so I love new agents getting into the business and focusing on affordability. We love training them up to pre-qualify renters because most of the time the renters don’t know they can buy a house. So it’s a great way to start your real estate business.

And in our company, we have a lot of things that sort of reinforce that culture of homeownership as the most impactful thing you can do in a community. We also create programs in-house that help leverage gift funds to just get people across the line, which I’ll talk about more, but we thread it through the entire “gestalt” of our organization.

John Featherston: What are some of the ground-level tactics that you’re using in your organization?

Katey McGrath: One of the things we do is we train up. If you get a call for a rental, find out if they are capable of qualifying for homeownership. We lean on our lenders. I rely on them and have a high level of expectation that they’re going to understand the down payment programs and the grant programs and the ability to stack them. We have a program called Building Equity where we crowdfund it. The partners of the company seeded it and now every agent in my company gives $5 to $50 every time they sell a house. We have a nice little fund, and we make a gift to anyone who buys a house for $250,000 or less in the city of Philadelphia. The only question we ask is, are you going to move into it?

We find that we can leverage that. If our lenders want to participate in the program and be on our website, they have to match that gift. We just want to keep the level of homeownership in Philadelphia as high as possible. And we also want people to consider other neighborhoods, other house sizes and conditions that maybe the people saving up for their dream homes are not looking at.

John Featherston: Ennis, how do you educate agents to help them find homes their buyers afford?

Ennis Antoine: When talking to my agents, I have to remind them first, you have to learn to stack resources. And what that means is, get involved in the city, the county and third-party companies like Georgia Dreams and ask them, “What programs do you have available to assist with down payment assistance?” In Atlanta, we have a program where the mayor wants to have 20,000 affordable homes built by 2030, so he has instructed his people to have this agency set aside funds to help buyers with down payment assistance; you have to live in our community for five years and it’s forgivable where you don’t have to pay back those funds. The goal is educating your agents on what funds are available and then once they’re educated, educate the buyers on what to expect and to set realistic expectations.

John Featherston: Are you seeing or anticipating any improvement in affordability issues from the ROAD to Housing Act?

Ennis Antoine: I chaired the FPC advisory committee (Federal Political Coordinators under NAR), and we worked on that bill for two years and got it passed. Now here’s the key, though. It is only an incentive. It’s going to take each one of us to inform our city councilmen and mayors on what’s available, and to pass these bills to say, “Hey, listen, how can we incentivize people to buy a home?” And then second, when it comes to housing supply, that’s going to take a while because we have an inventory shortage. It’s not going to happen overnight, but we have to be patient because it’s only a framework on what could happen if we partner with our city council and Realtor® organizations.

John Featherston: Ken, why is it critical to approach the affordability issue as far as you can see? And is it relevant to the specific markets that you’re now serving?

Ken Baris: Affordability is relative. Somebody who says “I can’t afford” is maybe a kid who grew up in a town, can’t afford to be in the town now, but they may be able to afford in another community. It’s being able to understand the benefits people can get. So for instance, Bank of America’s community reinvestment program with a grant of $17,500. We have a mortgage partnership, and we make sure anyone who will qualify for that is going to get that grant and use Bank of America because it’s good sense for the clients.

And if you are really astute about the business, you have people who are tenants—they don’t know they can afford to purchase. You can train people to purchase. You can help people improve their credit: Higher credit score, lower interest rate. You can train people to do things like say, “I will fall in like with four properties. I will not fall in love with one.” Because if you fall in like with four and we make four lower offers, we actually can turn you into a buyer and something more affordable by being willing to present offers. So we inspire a team to do the work and take the time and good things happen for clients.

We use foyersavings.com. A very interesting website; it has three things. Number one, it gives you an ability to save money at an okay interest rate or a good interest rate so that your money builds. Number two, it gives a modest down payment assistance with $600 credit of the first $10,000 you have, you get 6% additional in interest back. That’s not huge, but it’s something.

And three, it shows programs from all over—banks, lenders, community program—that provide grants. You may not know all the programs in your own market that are available. Foyer goes after these programs and makes them available to people that use the site. So it’s just being aware of these things, using your method of communication to get the information out, inspiring people to understand what they can do. If you don’t buy somewhere, you’re going to make somebody else wealthier.

John Featherston: A follow up to that, because you’re going into a lot of the nuances that help new buyers enter the marketplace. Have you made a concerted effort within your firm to make this type of training and education a competitive differentiator in your organization?

Ken Baris: Hugely. I find units to be sexy, not just high prices. And if you have salespeople that are in more affordable communities and they’re trained for these programs, they do better. Another thing that we’ll do is we’ll send out emails of successful buyers. “John thought he was going to rent. We let him know that we thought he could purchase, and the good news for John is we were right. You might be in the same position. Let’s get together.” And that’s the kind of communication we’re doing. I can’t change somebody’s income, but I could help them learn how to save more, how to improve their credit and how to get down payment assistance. $17,500 can make somebody from not a buyer to a buyer. And it’s a gift. It’s not a loan.

John Featherston: How are you and your agents getting past the current rhetoric that we hear among young people when they say they’re never going to be able to buy a home?

Katey McGrath: One of the biggest myths is that you think you need 20% down. And so it’s education, education, education, myth busting, destigmatizing these programs. It’s super important for young people in your community, but also make sure that your agents feel that way. And it’s great because like I said, the younger agents eat it up and it keeps them busy early in their career.

Ennis Antoine: I put pen to paper. So as far as paying $2,000 a month in rent, I’m saying, let’s talk about this for a second. A landlord just received $24,000 from you for one year. You say I’m staying there for three or four years. Then you have nothing to show for it. Whereas if you bought a home or a condominium, you pay this amount each month, you would have a tax write off and within four or five years, you’ll see a 4% or 5% increase in the value of the property. You can sell that property, walk away with cash, get the tax write off on your tax returns. And so if it was me, I would buy and invest and start to build wealth.

And if you build wealth, you can get a larger home and pay less money. So the key here is you’re a smart person. Let’s make a smart decision. Let’s buy.

Keith Smith: I want to pivot a little bit. We’re talking about how we can make a difference. Just last year through a land trust we put together 40 permanent affordable new construction units. I’m in Charlottesville with the second-highest cost of living in the state of Virginia, the second-highest cost of housing in Virginia. But we were able to do 40 of them. And the way we did this is what I call the four pillars: The local government, the private sector folks—developers, builders, real estate agents, the nonprofits and the people all of us serve. You got to get them into a room. You’ve got to get them all to go into the conversation. We put buyers and sellers together. We negotiate deals together. We put people together that maybe do not want to talk to one another, but they talk to people that get to the end result. And how you put those four pillars together is you show up to the meetings and you do what we all do every day very well, which is negotiate and put people together.

John Featherston: Why isn’t the real estate community playing a more pivotal role than every one of the communities, perhaps the most critical role as far as supporting homeownership?

Katey McGrath: I think everybody in this room is a connector. It’s what we love about what we do. And I think that our credibility and our expertise can help save money in these instances. The earlier we get involved in these conversations, the less mistakes the people with good intentions are going to make to make things more expensive. But also, the credibility that we have as a community member, right? So people are coming to us to buy houses, people are coming to us for education, people are coming to us to build generational wealth for their family. And then we can go to city council, we can go to the state reps, we can go to the zoning meetings and add all of that to just sort of be both sides of the issue.

Housing is bipartisan, so if you can get people together, you have that credibility, everything just becomes more productive and less expensive.

John Featherston: Getting people together over the issue of housing is a common denominator all of us can agree on. When Ennis said, local teachers, first responders, police, essential services, can’t afford to live in the community they’re serving, that is not a unique problem. That’s a problem that permeates around the nation. So the solutions have to be done locally.

Ennis Antoine: That’s correct. So I remind everyone, it doesn’t matter what company you work for, there is a percentage in every company where you deal with first-time homebuyers. It doesn’t have to be your main part of your business, but it should be a part of your business because to whom much is given, much is required. And we must always lead by example because the goal here is homeownership. What can we do? It’s all an education process. In every office, there are agents who are very passionate about their community. Support them, enhance them, show up when they need some help.

They will find a surgeon to have vibrant communities. We need a mixture of people in the community who are willing to work together, live together because we call it a village. And as real estate professionals, we are the fiber of the community. We are the voice of real estate and private property rights do matter.

Ken Baris: Something interesting we did some years ago, we listed 300 brand new two-family homes in Newark, New Jersey. And they were beautiful. The challenge was getting people in. So we had the builder prearrange financing, and we had them buy down the rate. And so it was a much lower interest rate, which lowered the payments. And then we also had the builder give a brand-new computer to every purchaser for one of the units because many of them were going to have kids and they would not have money left over for a new computer. And we thought that was very important. And then when certain buyers were tight, we then created a program where they were giving 5% toward closing costs, and if you get people to pay money toward closing costs, you also make it more affordable.

Keith Smith: “Connected” was the right word. I’ve been in this space for 15 years, and I would hear from elected officials, “Well, I don’t understand what the developer is saying.” The developer’s saying, “I don’t understand what the elected official is saying.” And then the nonprofits don’t understand anybody, and the poor folks that we’re trying to serve are left out there in the dark. Being a connector, that is the perfect word. That’s what we do. We connect and are able to put those four pillars together and put a developer and an elected official who really wants to do the right thing, together. The seller doesn’t trust the buyer; the buyer doesn’t trust the seller. We connect and we put people together and just get that conversation rolling. That’s how you do 40 new construction units in the second-highest cost-of-living area in the state of Virginia and everybody walks away smiling. I didn’t do anything really genius. I just put people in the room and said, start talking.

John Featherston: If you could do one thing to help move this affordability issue forward, what would you do?

Ennis Antoine: The one thing I would do is educate my colleagues and challenge them to get involved. It’s easy to write a check, but it’s amazing what happens when you show up. As a leader, when we show up, our people will follow. So as leaders, show up.

Ken Baris: I think just doing a better job of educating consumers because there’s a lot of buyers that don’t know their buyers. Not everyone will be able to afford. They’ve never always been able to, but there’s many more out there.

Katey McGrath: I’m going to go a little more philosophical. Just remember how important homeownership is to every metric in the community. It reduces crime. It increases education rates. It can lower the temperature in a zip code. It extends life expectancy, but most importantly, it builds generational wealth and creates health outcomes in that community that lift everybody up. And if you internalize that, you’re going to be happier when you go to work. You’re going to have more patience to deal with the hard clients that you’re not going to make a lot of money on and just feel great at the end of the day.

Keith Smith: Invest the one asset you can’t make more of, which is your time. Show up and over time, you’ll make a difference. And of those affordable housing units, every single key I handed to somebody, they were in tears. They never thought they were going to get into the homeownership game. It’s not about the check. It’s about the tears, and it makes a difference.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5582. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5581. The concessions field problem that breaks pay-for-listing data models

Contribution schemes that credit MLS data by listing totals overlook whether key valuation inputs are complete. A single MLS can require a numeric concessions amount whenever concessions are yes, improving downstream appraisal and model reliability.  AI Summary

Metering who uses listing data is an engineering problem with engineering answers. Deciding what a contributed listing is worth is not, and the difficulty sits in the field definitions rather than in anybody’s policy.

The proposal itself is sound, and it is gaining ground. Meter extraction, credit the organizations that supply the data, and reward the brokerages that send more of their eligible inventory into the system rather than less. Paper agreements stop working the moment data leaves the system, and an incentive attached to the record travels wherever the record goes.A contribution model based primarily on listing counts risks rewarding volume rather than the completeness and usefulness of the information. That is the obvious unit, and it is the wrong one, because two listings entered on the same morning by the same brokerage can differ by the only thing a valuation needs.

The RESO Data Dictionary permits three answers to whether a closed sale carried concessions: yes, no and call listing agent. The ‘Concessions Amount’ sits beside it as a number field, ‘Concessions Comments’ as free text. All three belong to the closing group, which RESO describes as intended to describe facts that occurred at the closing of a transaction rather than offers made before it. RESO’s own guidance says recording this data consistently is important, and notes that adopting the newer concessions fields is optional for any organization.A concession is consideration. Fannie Mae specifically says concessions adjustments should reflect their impact on the transaction price, rather than automatically deducting the full dollar amount of concessions. In some cases, the market-based adjustment may be smaller than the concession or unnecessary. Also, RESO’s concessions fields for closed transactions shouldn’t be confused with fields advertising potential seller concessions before closing.

RESO explicitly distinguishes the two uses in its April 2024 guidance. It moves the figure a buyer paid without moving the figure the deed records, and that gap is the entire reason an appraiser adjusts for it. Fannie Mae requires adjustments to reflect the market’s reaction to the difference between properties, naming paired sales as one method among statistical analysis, modeling and other commonly accepted approaches. Every one of them needs the magnitude.

It is not one field. View carries 38 category words, among them ‘Bay’, ‘City Lights’, ‘Ocean’ and ‘Panoramic’, with no amount and no rating attached. ‘Entry Level’ carries the floor as a number and nothing joins the two, while Fannie Mae’s condo section requires special attention to a unit’s location within its project and says nothing about view at all.So, a contribution model priced by record count pays for the half of the work that costs nothing. An address, bedrooms, bathrooms and a price make a record. The concession amount, the extent of the view and the condition detail make it evidence. Paying the same for both, or partial credit for the thinner one, is a reliable way to end up with more records rather than better ones.

I think requiring a number whenever the answer to the concessions question is ‘yes’ is a rules change inside a single MLS’s authority, enforceable at the point of entry, and it costs an agent the half minute it takes to read a closing statement already in front of them. Apply it to the other fields that carry magnitude rather than category and a contribution model has something worth metering.The alternative is a market that pays for volume. Records multiply, credits clear and the fields that decide what a house is worth carry whatever they happen to carry, because nothing in the scheme ever asked for them.The governance conversation is about who may read the record. What the record contains is a separate question, and it is the one that can be answered this quarter by any organization willing to make a single field mandatory.Nikola Gojkovic is the founder of CMAflow and writes on residential valuation methodology.
