#5541. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5540. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

#5538. Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5535. Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 9:51 amOctober 28, 2026 at 10:17 am

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan.

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”

T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

#5534. Supermicro and Arista Networks crush expectations as AI infrastructure wins again

Growing nervousness about spending on the artificial intelligence boom has made technology stocks increasingly volatile this year, but all it takes is one good quarter to reignite investor confidence, as Super Micro Computer Inc. and Arista Networks Inc. both showed today.

The companies are still relatively small fry in terms of the bigger AI picture, but as key data center infrastructure providers, they have shown consistently strong revenue growth over the last couple of years, and neither looks to be slowing down.

Indeed, Supermicro’s sales shot up by an incredible 298% in its latest quarter as it powered its way to yet another impressive revenue beat. The server maker reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.81 per share on sales of $19.95 billion, cruising past Wall Street’s guidance of $1.23 per share in earnings and $17.35 billion in sales. After-hours, the company’s stock gained more than 6%.

Meanwhile, Arista delivered third-quarter earnings of $1.20 per share on revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58% from a year earlier, surpassing the Street’s target of $1.08 per share in earnings and $3.33 billion in revenue. Its stock moved higher too, and rose more than 9% in the late-trading session. The company is a major supplier of networking equipment for AI data centers, helping to link together massive clusters of graphics processing units and other high-powered chips.

Supermicro Chief Executive Charles Liang (pictured) said his company continues to sell its servers and storage solutions as fast as it can build them. “Supermicro’s transformation into a total AI and IT data center solution provider continues to accelerate,” he added.

Investors were looking for signs that Supermicro may face headwinds in the coming months, with the impact of rising component costs being one of their major concerns. But the company’s results seem to have reassured doubters that supply issues could impact its profitability. Notably, Supermicro said its gross margin rose to 12.8% in the quarter, higher than the 9.3% margin recorded in the same quarter one year ago.

Supermicro’s guidance for the current quarter was impressive too. The company said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.66 and $1.90 per share on sales of between $19.5 billion and $21.5 billion in its second quarter. That’s much higher than the Street’s forecast, which calls for earnings of $1.14 per share and sales of $18.1 billion.

Arista’s 58% revenue growth was the biggest year-over-year jump since the company went public back in 2014, and it could well break that record again if its guidance holds true. The company said it’s looking for fourth-quarter earnings of between $1.26 and $1.30 per share on sales of $3.95 billion at the midpoint of its range. That would represent growth of 59%. The guidance was better than expected, with Wall Street looking for earnings of just $1.16 per share on sales of $3.65 billion.

Arista Chairperson and Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal told analysts that even she was surprised by how well the company did in the prior quarter. “This strong momentum across customer sectors highlights our increased relevance for the generative and agentic AI era,” she said.

NEW YORK, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fractal Analytics Ltd (BSE: 544700) (NSE: FRACTAL), an enterprise AI company that builds its own AI models, platforms and products for Fortune 500Â® organizations, announced its consolidated financial results for Q2 FY27, ending September 30, 2026.

#5532. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5531. /C O R R E C T I O N - Chord/

In the news release, Chord Expands into Enterprise AI With Zenlytic Acquisition, Adding Verizon, J.Crew, Domino's, and Stanley Black & Decker as Customers, issued 03-Nov-2026 by Chord over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

NEW YORK, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Chord, the AI native data platform for commerce, announced its acquisition of Zenlytic, an AI-powered business intelligence platform, doubling its revenue and adding a customer portfolio that includes Verizon, J.Crew, Domino's, and Stanley Black & Decker.

The acquisition accelerates Chord's expansion beyond commerce brands to address a growing challenge in enterprise businesses: giving agents access to data is easier than ensuring they understand the business. As definitions, metrics, and financial goals change, Chord keeps that context current, enforces permissions, and gives companies oversight of the answers their agents produce as AI scales across teams.

This was a strategic acquisition as Chord and Zenlytic went to market to solve the same problem: making AI reliable on company data. Chord built an end-to-end context layer for commerce brands, while Zenlytic developed an approach that works across industries on existing enterprise data warehouses. Bringing Zenlytic's technology and key team members into Chord accelerates that shared mission, helping more companies adopt and scale AI across the organization.

As AI becomes central to how enterprises and brands operate, companies need a reliable way to move from individual experiments to agents that work across the business. Without shared definitions and controls, teams can receive conflicting answers from the same data, spend time verifying results, and struggle to turn AI adoption into measurable business value.

"As enterprises and commerce brands make AI core to their operations, they're facing a critical decision about who controls the data and knowledge that make their businesses unique," said Bryan Mahoney, co-founder and CEO of Chord. "We saw what happened in commerce when brands became dependent on Facebook and Google to reach their own customers. Now, as OpenAI and Anthropic become central to how businesses use AI, there's a risk of repeating that same dependency with enterprise data and intelligence. Companies shouldn't have to hand over control of their most valuable business context to benefit from AI. Bringing Zenlytic into Chord gives them the infrastructure to own that context, keep it current, and use it across whichever AI models they choose."

Chord addresses this data challenge by giving teams and agents a shared, governed understanding of the business that stays current as it changes. This foundation helps companies expand AI across functions while retaining control of their data and the flexibility to adopt new models as the technology evolves.

"We built Zenlytic to help enterprises get answers they can trust from their own data, with a developer-first approach to keeping business context accurate," said Ryan Janssen, CEO at Zenlytic. "This transaction allows Chord to build on that work, combining our analytics engine with their data infrastructure and activation capabilities so customers can move from asking questions to acting on the answers."

Chord is the analytics harness between AI and company data, helping enterprises across industries scale AI with answers and actions they can trust. Combining data ingestion, AI-powered analytics and activation, Chord works with companies' existing data warehouses to turn natural-language questions into reliable answers and enable agents to act across business channels. The platform maintains business context and governed metrics, applies existing permissions, validates queries, and gives data teams visibility into agent activity. Founded in 2021, Chord is based in New York.

#5530. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5528. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5526. Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation

Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.

The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.

AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.

According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.

Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.

“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.

Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.

Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.

Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.

In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.

Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.

Kleiner Perkins’ Aditya Naganath said Traversal is the first company he has seen that brings “real intelligence” into complex production environments, and he’s confident there’s going to be enormous demand for it. “As AI dramatically accelerates the pace at which software is written and shipped, the complexity of managing production will only grow,” he predicted. “Traversal gives engineering teams the intelligence they need to understand their systems, resolve incidents faster and operate with confidence at scales that simply weren’t possible before.”

#5525. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5524. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5522. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5520. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5518. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5517. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5514. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5513. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

#5512. Montana voters take on Citizens United with a ballot initiative to strip corporations and nonprofits of their political spending power

Sixteen years ago, the Supreme Court decided in the Citizens United case that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend money to influence elections. On Tuesday, Montana voters will decide whether their state can take that power away.

Initiative 194, also known as the Montana Plan, would strip corporations, trade associations, nonprofits, and other organizations of the legal power to spend money supporting or opposing a political candidate or ballot initiative in Montana. Backers say they’ve found a way around Citizens United, while critics argue the semantics of the ballot initiative still violate the 2010 Supreme Court ruling.

Rather than ban corporate political donations outright, I-194 would change the powers Montana grants to corporations and other entities it refers to as “artificial persons,” limiting them to only those powers that are “necessary and convenient.”

The measure would apply to entities that do business or hold property in Montana, but exempts political action committees (PACs), news and editorial content, and individuals. Organizations that violate this would forfeit the privileges Montana grants them to do business in the state, including limited liability, which protects owners from personal responsibility for business debts.

At first glance, the language of the ballot initiative looks like it contradicts what Citizens United established—that corporations can spend money on elections. But Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen Weintraub and now senior fellow at the Center for American Progress (who also devised the legal theory behind the Montana Plan), told Fortune that states have authority over what corporations can do through corporate law.

“When the state creates a corporation, it is starting from nothing and deciding what to give the corporation, and no case has ever held that they have to give local spending power to a corporation,” Moore said.

He said I-194 would no longer grant corporations and nonprofits the ability to spend money on elections, which is different from banning them from exercising an existing right.

“It’s not regulation; it’s redefinition,” Moore said.

He said he believes the measure would shut down dark money spending by preventing wealthy donors from hiding behind organizations that don’t disclose their contributors. For instance, a donor can give money to a nonprofit that then funnels it to a PAC, which would report the nonprofit as the donor rather than identifying the person. Moore said I-194 would cut off that route by preventing corporations, nonprofits, and trade associations from political giving, though individuals can still donate.

“This is not going to stop Elon Musk from writing a big fat check to some election in Montana,” Moore said. “What it will stop them from doing is laundering the money through a dark money group.”

But opponents of the ballot measure say the distinction between banning corporations from political giving and exercising their political rights is blurry. Bradley Smith, a former FEC chairman and professor at Capital University Law School, told Fortune states can’t sidestep the First Amendment by calling political spending a corporate power instead of a right.

“The Supreme Court isn’t engaged in a semantic game,” he said.

Smith said states can set rules for corporations, but they can’t make them surrender constitutional protections in exchange for the benefits of incorporation.

“The core centerpiece undoubtedly is we’re going to deny all corporations in the state the right to speak about political affairs and about political candidates, and that’s just going to fail,” he said.

Montana has tried curbing corporate influence in elections before. In 1912, Montanans passed the Corrupt Practices Act by initiative with 76% of the vote, angry at the political power of mining giant Amalgamated Copper, years after the state’s mining magnates, known as the Copper Kings, had bribed state legislators.

The law barred corporations from spending money to influence elections, but the Supreme Court struck down the restriction in American Tradition Partnership v. Bullock in 2012, ruling that it conflicted with Citizens United.

Montana also isn’t the only state trying to limit corporate influence over elections. Hawaii enacted a law similar to I-194, called Act 11, in May. It’s now facing two federal lawsuits: one from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and another from the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, which the Institute for Free Speech, an organization Smith founded, represents. The cases could help decide whether states can use corporate law to restrict political spending despite Citizens United.

Moore expects the issue to go up to the Supreme Court, whether through I-194 or the Hawaii lawsuits. If voters approve I-194, it would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, unless a court blocks it.
