#5490. How to Decide Whether to Build In-House, Buy an Existing Solution or Partner With Another Company

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When should a company build, buy or partner? Here’s what you need to know.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

The details and economics widely vary, but the strategic question underneath is consistent. Companies should assess what they actually need and then work towards the best answer to fulfill that need based on a larger strategic vision.

Building internally makes sense when a capability is sufficiently important to competitive differentiation that management wants to control how it evolves.

This can apply to technology, intellectual property, operating processes or specialized expertise. If a capability determines why a customer chooses the company over competitors, then an outside provider may limit the ability of the company to differentiate. Internal development allows the company to shape the capability around its strategy rather than shaping its strategy around what the market offers.

Leaders, however, generally underestimate what “build” entails. Building does not end when a system launches, the new steam is assembled or the capability becomes operational. The organization has also chosen to maintain it, staff it, improve it and keep it relevant as the business changes. A company may have the capital to build a function, but it requires continued management attention, technical talent and operating discipline.

Buying can compress years of development work. In simple terms, that means purchasing an established technology platform or service rather than creating one internally. At the other end of the spectrum, it can mean acquiring a company because the desired capability, people, intellectual property, customers, volume, distribution or market position can be difficult to produce organically.

The financial analysis of an acquisition naturally focuses on purchase price, expected return, opportunity cost and integration challenges. Strategically, management should also determine exactly what it is buying and why. What value is the company trying to solve through inorganic growth or acquisition?

The second stage of buying includes integration. A company can acquire an asset immediately without immediately acquiring the ability to use the new asset well. Systems may have to connect, processes may change, and employees may need to adopt an entirely new operating model. The objective is to determine what advantage buying produces and how quickly it can be absorbed and transitioned into an operating advantage.

The third option is partnership. This approach allows companies to access expertise, distribution, technology or operating capabilities without assuming full ownership. That can be particularly useful when the capability matters to the customer proposition but does not itself need to become a core institutional competency.

Financial services provide many examples of this logical framework. Banks and finance companies frequently leverage technology providers, payment systems, capital providers, third-party complementary products or specialized services. Creating these components internally would consume enormous resources without necessarily improving what makes the company distinctive.

The same logic applies beyond financial services. A manufacturer may partner for logistics. A technology company may rely on specialized infrastructure. A growing business may use an outside provider for a function that would be expensive to build but does not meaningfully distinguish the company in the market.

Partnerships work best when companies have clearly defined value propositions and can find mutually beneficial arrangements that add value.

A disciplined build-buy-partner decision can be organized around several questions.

First, how important is this capability to differentiation? The closer it sits to the reason customers choose the company, the stronger the argument for ownership or significant control.

Second, how quickly does the organization need it? Build may produce a better long-term fit but arrive after the market opportunity has passed. Buying or partnering can create speed when timeliness matters.

Third, does the company possess the talent to own it? Capital alone doesn’t create capability. Management has to attract, retain and lead the people who operationalize ideas.

Fourth, what is full economics? Build costs include maintenance and continued development. Acquisition costs include integration. Partnerships may require recurring payments.

Fifth, how much control does the business actually need? Leaders sometimes demand ownership when contractual rights, service standards or a well-designed partnership would provide sufficient control at a substantially lower organizational cost.

Finally, what does this choice require the company to become? Every internal capability creates another area that leadership must manage well. Every acquisition adds complexity. Every partnership creates an external dependency that must be governed.

Each of the three options has pros and cons that largely depend on the functional needs of the business. There is no right option when costs and opportunities coexist, depending on the company’s strategy and fundamentals. The main point is that all three options require careful analysis and thought before operationalizing.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

#5489. James Talarico wasn’t born the last time a Democrat won a Texas Senate race. At 37, he won one despite $200 million from Elon Musk to stop him

Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas’s Senate race, NBC News and Decision Desk HQ projected. The 37-year-old is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988, when Lloyd Bentsen won his last term, six months before Talarico was born. He is also the first Democrat to win any statewide office there since 1994.

Elon Musk spent more than $200 million to help elect Paxton, according to a New York Times analysis cited in Fortune’s tally of his political giving. Most of it went through the Senate GOP’s main super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund. Musk gave SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23, and each time, SLF moved nearly the same amount into a new entity called Texas PAC the next day, the Texas Tribune reported. His trust also gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, the main outside group backing Paxton.

The money came after Talarico had outspent Paxton on the airwaves for months. By the end of September, outside groups led by SLF had spent more than $217 million on ads in the race. Trump’s main super PAC added $10 million, its first major outlay of the midterms.

Talarico relied mostly on his own campaign. By early September he had raised $72 million to Paxton’s $16.8 million, and he finished the cycle as the most prolific fundraiser in the country. He made Musk’s spending part of his message. “This Senate seat doesn’t belong to Elon Musk,” he said on the trail.

Paxton reached the general election by beating Sen. John Cornyn, a four-term incumbent, in the May runoff. He won by nearly 28 points after Trump endorsed him. Cornyn had warned that a Paxton nomination could cost Republicans $150 million to $200 million to hold the seat, the Texas Tribune reported. Paxton was impeached by the Texas House on bribery and corruption allegations in 2023 and acquitted by the state Senate. After losing the runoff, Cornyn called Paxton “lazy” and said he would help Republicans elsewhere instead of raising money for him. Paxton never agreed to debate Talarico, making this the first Texas Senate race since 2000 without a debate between the major-party nominees.

Talarico, a state legislator and Presbyterian seminarian, ran on affordability and corruption. He argued that Paxton had served wealthy donors while Texans struggled with the cost of groceries, housing and health care. The race also turned on masculinity and anti-transgender attacks, the 19th reported.

It was the second time Tuesday night that a Republican whose path to the nomination ran through Trump lost a seat his party had held for decades. Earlier, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina.

Texans voted early in record numbers. Early voting reached 40.5% of registered voters, the highest midterm early-turnout rate on record in modern Texas. Talarico built his lead in the suburbs. In partial returns, he was winning Tarrant and Collin counties, which Trump carried by 5 and 11 points in 2024. Trump won Texas by 13.7 points two years ago.

#5488. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.
